questions.correct_answer: Interest that is added during the year also earns interest
questions.feedback: With compounding, earlier interest earns interest too, so the yearly yield is above the stated rate.

questions.intro: Most savings accounts have variable rates: the bank can raise or lower them, often when market interest rates change. A certificate of deposit usually locks a rate for its term.
questions.question: A savings rate is "variable." What does that mean?

choices.text: The bank can change the rate over time
The rate is fixed until the account is closed
The rate depends on how many times you log in
The rate is negative in some months

questions.correct_answer: The bank can change the rate over time
questions.feedback: Variable means the bank may change it; past or advertised rates are not promises.

questions.question: An ad shows "5.00% APY*", and the fine print says "*on balances up to $1,000; 0.50% APY on the amount above $1,000." Sara deposits $5,000. About how much interest will she earn in one year?

questions.section_skill: Deposit insurance limits and ownership categories
questions.intro: The $250,000 limit applies per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Money at two different banks is insured separately. (Two "brands" of the same bank are one bank for insurance purposes.)
questions.question: Marcus has $200,000 in an individual account at Bank A and $200,000 in an individual account at Bank B. Both banks are FDIC insured and separate. How much of his money is insured?

misconceptions.C: Applies one limit across different banks
misconceptions.A: Thinks large balances are never insured

questions.feedback: Each bank insures his $200,000 individually: $400,000 total.

questions.section_skill: Deposit insurance limits and ownership categories
questions.intro: Joint accounts are a separate ownership category from individual accounts. Each co-owner's share of joint accounts at one bank is insured up to $250,000.
questions.question: Sam and Pat own a joint account with $500,000 at one insured bank. Joint accounts are insured up to $250,000 per co-owner. How much is insured?

misconceptions.B: Applies one limit to the whole joint account

questions.feedback: Two co-owners × $250,000 = $500,000 of coverage, which covers the whole balance.

questions.section_skill: Deposit insurance limits and ownership categories
questions.question: Which product is covered by FDIC insurance when bought at an insured bank?

choices.text: The contents of a safe deposit box

questions.correct_answer: A 12-month certificate of deposit

misconceptions.A: Thinks funds sold at banks are insured
misconceptions.B: Thinks crypto at a bank is insured

questions.feedback: CDs are deposits. Investments, crypto assets, and safe deposit box contents are not insured deposits.

questions.section_skill: Deposit insurance limits and ownership categories
questions.intro: Only deposits at FDIC-insured banks (or NCUA-insured credit unions) are covered by deposit insurance. The FDIC warns consumers about companies that misrepresent their products as FDIC insured.
questions.question: A website for a company that sells crypto says, "Your funds are safe — like a bank." What should a careful saver conclude?

choices.text: The funds must be FDIC insured
The company is a federally chartered bank
The NCUA insures every crypto platform that operates in the United States
That claim does not mean the funds are FDIC insured

questions.correct_answer: That claim does not mean the funds are FDIC insured

misconceptions.A: Treats a comparison as a guarantee

questions.feedback: Comparisons to banks are not insurance. Check the FDIC's BankFind tool to see if an institution is an insured bank, and remember crypto assets are not deposits.

questions.section_skill: Deposit insurance limits and ownership categories
questions.question: Ella has $260,000 in one individual account at an insured bank and wants all of it insured. Which change would accomplish that most directly?

choices.text: Move $10,000 or more to an account at a different insured bank
Split it into two individual accounts at the same bank
Ask the bank to raise her personal limit
Withdraw the extra $10,000 and invest it in stocks for added safety

questions.correct_answer: Move $10,000 or more to an account at a different insured bank

misconceptions.B: Thinks multiple accounts in one category add coverage

questions.feedback: Coverage is per bank per category. Two individual accounts at the same bank share one $250,000 limit; a second bank adds coverage.

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.intro: A check is a written order telling your bank to pay someone from your account. You write the date, the payee (who gets paid), the amount in numbers, the amount in words with cents as a fraction of 100, and your signature. The words are the legal amount if the two differ.
questions.question: Nora writes a check for $1,254.07. How should she write the amount in words on the check?

choices.text: One thousand two hundred fifty-four and 07/100 dollars
One thousand two hundred fifty-four and 7/10 dollars
Twelve hundred fifty-four point zero seven
One thousand two hundred forty-five and 07/100 dollars

questions.correct_answer: One thousand two hundred fifty-four and 07/100 dollars

misconceptions.C: Uses "point" instead of the cents fraction

questions.feedback: $1,254.07 is written "One thousand two hundred fifty-four and 07/100 dollars."

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.intro: To deposit or cash a check made out to you, you "endorse" it by signing the back. Adding "For deposit only" (a restrictive endorsement) means the check can only be deposited, which protects it if it is lost. For mobile deposit, banks often require "For mobile deposit only" too.
questions.question: Ben receives a paycheck made out to him and wants to deposit it at an ATM. What should he write on the back?

choices.text: Nothing; endorsing a check is optional
His PIN, so the ATM can verify him
His account balance, so the bank can update it

questions.correct_answer: His signature and "For deposit only"

misconceptions.B: Writes sensitive data on a check
misconceptions.C: Thinks the balance goes on the check

questions.feedback: Signing with "For deposit only" endorses the check and limits it to being deposited.

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.intro: Peer-to-peer (P2P) payment apps move money quickly between people. Money you send yourself, even to a scammer, is usually treated as authorized and is often hard to get back. Federal error protections focus on transfers you did not authorize. Use P2P apps mainly with people you know and trust.
questions.question: Mia sends $60 through a payment app to someone selling concert tickets online. The tickets never arrive. Which statement is most accurate?

choices.text: The app must refund every payment that goes wrong
Her bank will reverse the payment automatically within one business day
The seller must legally deliver the tickets
Payments she authorized are often hard or impossible to reverse

questions.correct_answer: Payments she authorized are often hard or impossible to reverse

misconceptions.C: Thinks the law forces a scammer to deliver

questions.feedback: Because Mia authorized the payment, getting it back depends on the app's or bank's voluntary policies. Protections are stronger for unauthorized transfers.

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.intro: Mobile check deposit lets you photograph a signed check in your bank's app. The bank may hold part of the money for a few days. Keep the paper check until the deposit is final, then destroy it securely so it cannot be deposited twice or misused.
questions.question: After depositing a check with his phone, what should Kai do with the paper check?

choices.text: Keep it until the deposit is final, then destroy it
Deposit the same check again at the bank to be safe
Throw it in the trash right after taking the photo
Give it back to the person who wrote it

questions.correct_answer: Keep it until the deposit is final, then destroy it

misconceptions.C: Discards it before the deposit is confirmed

questions.feedback: Keep it until the funds are final in case the bank needs it, then shred it.

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.question: Zara's landlord asks for rent in a way that leaves a record of payment. Which method fits BEST?

choices.text: A check or an electronic transfer from her bank account
Cash handed over without a receipt
A gift card code sent by text
A wire transfer to an account number she has never verified

questions.correct_answer: A check or an electronic transfer from her bank account
questions.feedback: Checks and bank transfers leave records Zara can use as proof of payment.

questions.intro: Common ways to pay: cash; debit cards and checks (from your account); electronic transfers such as online bill pay and automatic payments (from your account, electronically); credit cards (borrowed money); and prepaid or gift cards (money loaded in advance).
questions.question: Which payment method moves money directly from your bank account electronically on a date you set?

choices.text: A paper check that the store mails to you each month
An online bill payment or automatic transfer

questions.correct_answer: An online bill payment or automatic transfer

misconceptions.B: Confuses borrowing with paying from your account
misconceptions.C: Confuses prepaid value with an account payment

questions.feedback: Online bill pay and automatic payments take money from your account electronically.

questions.intro: A payment record proves you paid. Bank statements, cleared checks, and confirmation numbers are records. Cash leaves no record unless you get a receipt.
questions.question: Which method gives the LEAST proof that you paid?

choices.text: A check that the bank later shows as cleared
A debit card purchase listed on the statement
An online bill payment with a confirmation number

questions.correct_answer: Cash with no receipt

misconceptions.A: A cleared check is a record

questions.feedback: Cash without a receipt leaves no proof of payment.

questions.intro: A prepaid or gift card holds a set amount of money. Each purchase is subtracted until the card reaches $0.
questions.question: A gift card loaded with $50 is used to buy a $12 item. What is left on the card?

misconceptions.C: Thinks the card balance does not change
misconceptions.A: Confuses the price with what is left

questions.question: Who is the "payee" on a check?

choices.text: The person or business that receives the money
The account holder who signs and writes the check
The bank that prints the check
The cashier who accepts the check

questions.correct_answer: The person or business that receives the money

misconceptions.B: Confuses payee with the account holder

questions.feedback: The payee is named on the "Pay to the order of" line.

questions.question: Which situation makes a payment app MOST risky to use?

choices.text: Paying a stranger online before receiving the item
Splitting a dinner bill with a close friend
Paying a family member back for groceries
Sending rent money to a roommate you have lived with for a year

questions.correct_answer: Paying a stranger online before receiving the item
questions.feedback: Paying strangers in advance is how many P2P scams work, because payments are hard to reverse.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: A wire transfer moves money between banks quickly, often the same day, and is generally final once sent. ACH transfers (used for direct deposit and online bill pay) move money between bank accounts more slowly and have some ways to return errors. Scammers often ask for wires because they are fast and hard to reverse.
questions.question: Which payment is generally the hardest to reverse once sent?

choices.text: A check that has not been cashed yet
A debit card purchase you did not authorize

questions.correct_answer: A wire transfer

misconceptions.B: A stop payment may be possible

questions.feedback: Wires are fast and generally final, which is why scammers prefer them.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: A cashier's check is drawn on the bank's own funds, so a real one is very reliable. But fake cashier's checks are common. The bank may make the money available before discovering the check is fake; when it bounces, you owe the bank the full amount.
questions.question: A buyer sends Liam a cashier's check for $1,500 for a $500 phone and asks him to wire back the extra $1,000. What is most likely happening?

choices.text: A generous buyer making an honest mistake
A normal practice for cashier's checks
A bank error that the bank will cover

questions.correct_answer: A fake-check scam

misconceptions.B: Ignores the classic overpayment scam pattern
misconceptions.D: Thinks the bank absorbs fraud losses

questions.feedback: Overpayment with a request to send money back is a classic fake-check scam. Liam would owe the bank when the check bounces.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: The ACH (Automated Clearing House) network moves money electronically between bank accounts in batches. It is cheaper and slower than a wire transfer.
questions.question: Which is a typical use of an ACH transfer?

choices.text: Paying a bill with a paper money order bought at a store
Swiping a credit card at a store
An employer's direct deposit of paychecks

questions.correct_answer: An employer's direct deposit of paychecks
questions.feedback: Direct deposit and many automatic bill payments use the ACH network.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: Criminals hack or fake emails and send new "updated" wire instructions so money goes to their account. Because wires are hard to reverse, verify instructions through a trusted phone number, not one in the suspicious email.
questions.question: Before wiring money for a home or apartment deposit, what is the safest step?

choices.text: Use the instructions in the most recent email, even if they changed
Wire the money quickly so you do not lose the apartment
Ask the sender to text you the account number again
Call a phone number you already know is real to confirm the instructions

questions.correct_answer: Call a phone number you already know is real to confirm the instructions

misconceptions.C: Uses the same possibly hacked channel

questions.feedback: Independent verification defeats changed-instructions scams.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: Until a check is paid by your bank, you can ask the bank not to pay it. Banks usually charge a fee for this service, and it does not work on a check that has already cleared.
questions.question: Ruth wrote a check and then learned it was lost in the mail before it was cashed. What service could stop it?

choices.text: A stop payment order through her bank
A wire recall, which works on all checks
Reporting the check to the IRS
Writing a second check for the same amount

questions.correct_answer: A stop payment order through her bank
questions.feedback: A stop payment order tells the bank not to pay that check, if it has not already cleared.

questions.intro: A common scam claims you received money "by mistake" and asks you to send it back. Sometimes the original payment was made with stolen information and is later reversed, leaving you with the loss. Verify inside your own app or bank, never through a link or message.
questions.question: Someone texts Ava: "I sent you $200 by mistake — please send it back!" Her app shows no new money in her account. What should she do?

choices.text: Check her own account directly and send nothing
Send $200 back right away to be polite
Reply with her bank login so they can fix it

questions.correct_answer: Check her own account directly and send nothing

misconceptions.D: Still sends money to a scammer

questions.feedback: Without verified money in her own account, there is nothing to return. Even if money did arrive, contact the app's support rather than sending money.

questions.question: Which setting adds the most protection to a payment app?

choices.text: Sharing your login with a parent and a friend so they can watch for fraud
Using the same password as your email
Multi-factor authentication and a passcode on the app

questions.correct_answer: Multi-factor authentication and a passcode on the app
questions.feedback: Multi-factor authentication and an app passcode make unauthorized access much harder.

questions.intro: Real banks and payment apps do not ask you to move money to a "safe account" to protect it. Imposters pretend to be bank staff, tech support, or government officials and create urgency.
questions.question: A "customer support" caller says your payment app is hacked and asks you to send your balance to a "safe account." What is this?

choices.text: A way to earn extra interest

questions.correct_answer: An imposter scam

misconceptions.A: Real companies do not ask this

questions.feedback: Any request to move money to protect it is a red flag for an imposter scam. Hang up and call the official number.

questions.question: Which payment is generally protected under federal error rules (Regulation E)?

choices.text: A transfer someone else made from your account without permission
A payment you chose to send to an online seller who never shipped
A payment you sent to the wrong person after typing their name
Money you lost gambling with an app

questions.correct_answer: A transfer someone else made from your account without permission
questions.feedback: Regulation E protections focus on unauthorized transfers and certain errors; payments you authorize, even to scammers, are often not covered.

questions.question: Before sending money with a payment app to someone new, which step lowers the risk the MOST?

choices.text: Sending a small test payment to a stranger
Checking that the stranger's profile has a photo and many friends
Asking the stranger to promise to deliver
Confirming who the recipient is through a source you trust

questions.correct_answer: Confirming who the recipient is through a source you trust
questions.feedback: Verifying who you are paying, through a channel you trust, prevents most P2P losses.

questions.section_skill: Calculate gross pay for hourly work, including overtime
questions.intro: An hourly wage is the amount paid for each hour of work. Gross pay is the total earned before taxes or any other deductions are taken out. For hourly work: gross pay = hourly wage × hours worked.
questions.question: Jada earns $16.50 per hour and works 24 hours this week. What is her gross pay for the week?

misconceptions.A: Adds the wage and the hours

questions.section_skill: Calculate gross pay for hourly work, including overtime
questions.intro: Federal law (the Fair Labor Standards Act) requires most hourly employees to be paid at least 1.5 times their regular rate for hours worked over 40 in a workweek. This is "time and a half." Hours up to 40 are paid at the regular rate.
questions.question: Malik is an hourly employee who earns $18 per hour. He works 46 hours in one workweek. Under the federal overtime rule, what is his gross pay?

misconceptions.A: Pays every hour at the regular rate
misconceptions.D: Pays every hour at the overtime rate

questions.feedback: Regular: 40 × $18 = $720. Overtime rate: $18 × 1.5 = $27. Overtime: 6 × $27 = $162. Total: $882.

questions.section_skill: Calculate gross pay for hourly work, including overtime
questions.intro: Paychecks show two key amounts. Gross pay is everything earned for the period. Net pay ("take-home pay") is what is left after deductions such as taxes and benefit costs, and it is what is actually deposited.
questions.question: Malik's pay stub shows "Gross pay: $882." What does gross pay mean?

choices.text: His total earnings before any deductions
The amount deposited into his bank account
His pay after taxes but before his retirement contribution
The overtime portion of his paycheck only

questions.correct_answer: His total earnings before any deductions

misconceptions.B: Confuses gross pay with net pay
misconceptions.C: Thinks gross pay is partly after deductions

questions.feedback: Gross pay is the total earned before deductions; net pay is what he takes home.

questions.section_skill: Calculate gross pay for hourly work, including overtime
questions.intro: Timecards often record hours in decimals: 15 minutes is 0.25 hour, 30 minutes is 0.5 hour, and 45 minutes is 0.75 hour. Add the hours first, then multiply by the hourly wage.
questions.question: Ana's timecard shows Monday 6.5 hours, Wednesday 4.25 hours, and Saturday 8 hours. She earns $15.20 per hour. What is her gross pay?

misconceptions.B: Drops the quarter hour and uses 18 hours

questions.section_skill: Calculate gross pay for hourly work, including overtime
questions.question: Two summer jobs require 30 hours a week. Job A pays $17.25 per hour. Job B pays a flat $500 per week. Which pays more per week, and by how much?
questions.correct_answer: Job A, by $17.50

misconceptions.C: Uses one hour's wage as the difference
misconceptions.D: Does not compute the hourly total

questions.intro: A wage is a rate: dollars per hour. The more hours you work, the more you earn.
questions.question: A job pays $14 per hour. What does that mean?

choices.text: The worker earns $14 for the whole day
The worker earns $14 per week no matter the hours
The worker pays $14 for each hour of training
The worker earns $14 for each hour worked

questions.correct_answer: The worker earns $14 for each hour worked

misconceptions.A: Confuses a wage with a daily amount
misconceptions.B: Confuses a wage with a weekly salary

questions.feedback: $14 per hour means $14 for every hour worked.

questions.intro: Earnings for hourly work = wage × hours.
questions.question: Rina earns $14 per hour and works 10 hours. How much does she earn?

questions.intro: An hour has 60 minutes. To change minutes to part of an hour, divide by 60: 15 ÷ 60 = 0.25.
questions.question: How many hours is 7 hours and 15 minutes, written as a decimal?
questions.correct_answer: 7.25 hours

misconceptions.A: Writes minutes as hundredths of an hour
misconceptions.B: Treats 15 minutes as half an hour

questions.feedback: 15 minutes = 15/60 = 0.25 hour, so 7 h 15 min = 7.25 hours.

questions.intro: "Gross" pay is the full amount earned. "Net" pay, also called take-home pay, is what remains after deductions.
questions.question: Which number on a paycheck shows earnings BEFORE taxes are taken out?
questions.correct_answer: Gross pay
questions.feedback: Gross pay is before deductions.

questions.intro: A raise in the hourly wage adds that amount for every hour worked.
questions.question: Leo's wage rises from $15 to $16 per hour. He works 20 hours a week. How much more does he earn each week?

misconceptions.A: Gives the raise per hour, not per week

questions.feedback: $1 more per hour × 20 hours = $20 more per week.

questions.intro: Federal overtime is based on hours in a WORKWEEK (any fixed, repeating 7-day period), not hours in a day. A few states also require daily overtime, so state law can add protection.
questions.question: Jon works 10 hours a day, Monday through Thursday, and no other hours that week. Under the federal rule, how many overtime hours does he earn?
questions.correct_answer: 0 hours

misconceptions.C: Counts one whole day as overtime

questions.feedback: 4 × 10 = 40 hours, which is not over 40 in the workweek, so there is no federal overtime. A state with daily overtime rules could require more.

questions.intro: Some salaried employees are "exempt" from overtime because they are paid at least a minimum salary and their main duties are executive, administrative, or professional. Being paid a salary alone does not make someone exempt; the duties test also matters.
questions.question: A salaried store manager meets the legal tests for an "exempt" employee and works 50 hours one week. What overtime pay does federal law require?

choices.text: Time and a half for the 10 extra hours
Double time for every hour over 40
One extra day off for each hour over 40

questions.correct_answer: No overtime pay is required
questions.feedback: Exempt employees are not entitled to overtime pay under federal law, even for long weeks.

questions.question: Pia earns $20 per hour and works 52 hours in a workweek. What is her gross pay?

misconceptions.A: Pays every hour at the regular rate
misconceptions.D: Pays every hour at time and a half

questions.intro: The federal overtime law does not require extra pay for holidays or weekends. Many employers offer holiday pay as a policy, and union contracts may require it, but that is not the federal rule.
questions.question: Does federal law require employers to pay time and a half for working on a holiday, when the week totals 32 hours?

choices.text: No; it depends on employer policy
Yes, if the employee asks for it in writing

questions.correct_answer: No; it depends on employer policy
questions.feedback: Holiday premium pay comes from employer policy or contracts, not the FLSA; at 32 hours, no overtime applies.

questions.question: Job A pays $19 per hour and usually schedules 45 hours a week (overtime applies). How much does Job A pay for a typical week?

misconceptions.A: Pays every hour at the regular rate
misconceptions.C: Pays the overtime hours at double time
misconceptions.D: Pays every hour at time and a half

questions.intro: In many restaurant jobs, pay has two parts: an hourly cash wage from the employer and tips from customers. Some states allow a lower cash wage for tipped workers (a "tip credit"), and others require the full minimum wage before tips.
questions.question: Kai, a server, worked 25 hours at a cash wage of $5.00 per hour and earned $410 in tips. What were his total earnings for the week?

misconceptions.C: Adds hours instead of wage × hours

questions.question: Kai earned $535 in wages and tips for 25 hours of work. What were his average earnings per hour?

questions.intro: Tips are taxable income. Employees who receive $20 or more in tips in a month must report them to their employer, who includes them in payroll records and withholding.
questions.question: Kai received $410 in tips this month. What does the IRS require?

choices.text: Nothing; tips are gifts and never taxed
He reports tips only in months when they exceed $1,000 in total
The customer reports the tips for him
He reports them to his employer; they are taxable

questions.correct_answer: He reports them to his employer; they are taxable
questions.feedback: Monthly tips of $20 or more must be reported to the employer, and tips are taxable.

questions.intro: When an employer pays a lower cash wage and counts tips toward the minimum wage, the employer must make up the difference if wages plus tips fall below the full minimum wage for the hours worked.
questions.question: In a state where the minimum wage is $15.00 per hour and a tip credit is allowed, Lia works 20 hours at a $5.00 cash wage and earns $150 in tips. Federal rules require her total to reach at least minimum wage for those hours. How much must her employer add?

misconceptions.C: Gives her tips as the amount owed

questions.feedback: Required: 20 × $15 = $300. She received $100 + $150 = $250. The employer must add $50.

questions.question: Kai's tips vary from $250 to $500 a week. Which budgeting approach is safest?

choices.text: Plan around a lower weekly amount and save the extra
Plan around his best week ever
Plan around the average and spend any extra right away
Ignore tips completely and skip budgeting

questions.correct_answer: Plan around a lower weekly amount and save the extra

misconceptions.C: Leaves no cushion for slow weeks

questions.feedback: With uneven income, budgeting on a conservative amount and saving surpluses smooths slow weeks.

questions.question: A full-time job pays a salary of $41,600 per year. Full-time is 40 hours a week for 52 weeks (2,080 hours). What is the equivalent hourly rate?

questions.intro: Pay frequency affects each paycheck's size: weekly = 52 paychecks per year; biweekly (every two weeks) = 26; semimonthly (twice a month, such as the 1st and 15th) = 24; monthly = 12.
questions.question: Ryan earns $41,600 a year, paid biweekly (every two weeks). What is his gross pay per paycheck?
questions.feedback: $41,600 ÷ 26 = $1,600.00 per biweekly paycheck.

questions.set_title: Salaries, hourly pay, and pay periods
questions.section_skill: Convert between annual salary, hourly pay, and pay per paycheck

questions.feedback: Semimonthly means 24 paychecks: $41,600 ÷ 24 = $1,733.33.

questions.intro: A year has 12 months but 52 weeks. Schedules based on weeks do not line up evenly with months, while schedules based on dates in the month always do.
questions.question: Which pay schedule gives a worker three paychecks in two months of most years?
questions.correct_answer: Biweekly (every two weeks)
questions.feedback: Biweekly pay gives 26 paychecks a year, so two months have three paychecks. Semimonthly is always two per month.

questions.question: How many weeks are in a year?
questions.feedback: A year has 52 weeks.

questions.question: Tom earns $500 a week. Which is the best estimate of his MONTHLY pay?
questions.correct_answer: About $2,167

questions.question: A job pays $2,400 per month. What is the yearly pay?

questions.question: What is a "salary"?

choices.text: Pay that changes with every hour worked
A bonus paid at the end of the year
A set yearly amount, paid in paychecks

questions.correct_answer: A set yearly amount, paid in paychecks
questions.feedback: A salary is a set annual amount paid in regular paychecks.

questions.correct_answer: Offer B, by $1,000

misconceptions.B: Pays overtime at the regular rate
misconceptions.A: Gives one week of overtime pay

questions.feedback: Overtime rate $28.50 × 5 hours = $142.50 per week; × 50 weeks = $7,125.

questions.section_skill: Comparing job offers by yearly pay
questions.question: Why should expected overtime be treated cautiously when comparing offers?

choices.text: Overtime hours may not be guaranteed and can change
Overtime is illegal in most jobs
Overtime always lowers your hourly rate

questions.correct_answer: Overtime hours may not be guaranteed and can change
questions.feedback: Overtime depends on the employer's needs. Base pay is more predictable.

questions.set_title: Salaries, hourly pay, and pay periods

questions.question: Two offers both pay $45,000. Offer D is paid monthly; Offer E is paid biweekly. Which statement is TRUE?

choices.text: Offer E pays more because there are more paychecks
Offer D pays more because each paycheck is larger
Offer E pays less because of extra processing
They pay the same per year

questions.correct_answer: They pay the same per year

misconceptions.A: Confuses more paychecks with more pay
misconceptions.B: Confuses paycheck size with yearly pay

questions.feedback: $45,000 is $45,000 either way: 12 checks of $3,750 or 26 checks of about $1,730.77.

questions.section_skill: Comparing job offers by yearly pay

questions.correct_answer: Offer F, by $500
questions.feedback: F: $40,000 + $3,000 = $43,000, which is $500 more than G's $42,500, but only if the bonus is paid.

questions.intro: Purchasing power is what your money can buy. If prices rise faster than your pay, your pay buys less, even though the number of dollars went up.
questions.question: Prices rose 4% the same year Noor got a 3% raise. What happened to what her pay can buy?
questions.correct_answer: It fell slightly
questions.feedback: A 3% raise with 4% inflation means her pay buys about 1% less than before.

questions.intro: Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
questions.question: Noor's pay rose from $46,350 to $48,204. What percent raise was this?

misconceptions.D: Uses the dollar change as a percent

questions.correct_answer: The bonus: $1,000 vs $800
questions.feedback: 2% of $40,000 = $800 for the next year, less than the $1,000 bonus. (A raise usually continues in later years, which a bonus does not.)

questions.section_skill: Read a pay stub and calculate deductions and net pay
questions.intro: A pay stub (pay statement) shows: gross pay; deductions, which are amounts taken out for taxes, retirement, insurance, and more; net pay, which is gross pay minus deductions; and year-to-date (YTD) totals. Net pay is your take-home pay.
questions.question: Which amount on a pay stub is the money actually deposited into the worker's bank account?
questions.correct_answer: Net pay

misconceptions.C: Confuses this period with the year total
misconceptions.D: Confuses money taken out with money received

questions.feedback: Net pay = gross pay − deductions, and it is the amount deposited.

questions.section_skill: Read a pay stub and calculate deductions and net pay
questions.intro: FICA taxes fund Social Security and Medicare. Employees pay 6.2% of wages for Social Security (up to a yearly wage limit) and 1.45% for Medicare. The employer pays a matching amount.
questions.question: Gabriel's gross pay is $1,200.00. The Social Security tax rate for employees is 6.2%. How much Social Security tax is withheld?

questions.section_skill: Read a pay stub and calculate deductions and net pay
questions.question: Gabriel's gross pay is $1,200.00. The Medicare tax rate for employees is 1.45%. How much Medicare tax is withheld?

questions.section_skill: Read a pay stub and calculate deductions and net pay
questions.intro: To find net pay, add all the deductions, then subtract the total from gross pay. Retirement contributions are deductions too, even though the money is still yours in a retirement account.
questions.question:
Pay stub (biweekly): Gross pay $1,200.00 | 401(k) contribution (pre-tax) $60.00 | Federal income tax $88.00 | Social Security $74.40 | Medicare $17.40 | State income tax $22.80
What is Gabriel's net pay?

misconceptions.A: Gives total deductions instead of net pay

questions.section_skill: Read a pay stub and calculate deductions and net pay
questions.intro: Deductions go to different places. Income taxes and Social Security and Medicare taxes are sent to the government. Retirement plan contributions are deposited into an account in the worker's name.
questions.question:
Pay stub (biweekly): Gross pay $1,200.00 | 401(k) contribution (pre-tax) $60.00 | Federal income tax $88.00 | Social Security $74.40 | Medicare $17.40 | State income tax $22.80
Which deduction is money Gabriel still owns after it leaves his paycheck?
questions.correct_answer: The 401(k) contribution

misconceptions.A: Thinks withheld tax is still his
misconceptions.C: Thinks withheld tax is still his

questions.feedback: A 401(k) contribution goes into his own retirement account. Taxes withheld are paid to the government (any overpaid income tax comes back as a refund).

questions.intro: Many workers have their paychecks deposited into bank accounts. The amount deposited is net pay: gross pay minus deductions such as taxes and benefit costs. Gross pay is what you earned; net pay is what you receive.
questions.question: Ivy's job offer says "$18 per hour." Her first paycheck is smaller than 18 × her hours. Why?

choices.text: Deductions were taken from her gross pay
Her employer made an error by paying less than promised
The bank charged a fee for depositing her paycheck
Her hourly wage was lowered in her first week

questions.correct_answer: Deductions were taken from her gross pay

misconceptions.B: Expects net pay to equal gross pay

questions.feedback: Deductions explain the difference between gross pay (18 × hours) and net pay.

questions.intro: Net pay = gross pay − total deductions.
questions.question: Gross pay $500. Deductions $85. What is net pay?

questions.intro: Gross pay = net pay + deductions.
questions.question: Net pay is $640 and deductions are $160. What was gross pay?
Ivy earns $18 per hour, but her take-home pay is less after deductions. Which amount should she use to plan her monthly spending?
questions.correct_answer: Her net pay

misconceptions.A: Budgets with money she never receives
misconceptions.B: Uses an estimate of gross pay

questions.feedback: Budgets are built on take-home (net) pay, the money she actually has.

questions.question: Which item is a deduction, NOT part of gross pay?
questions.correct_answer: Federal income tax withheld
questions.feedback: Withheld taxes are deductions. Overtime, wages, and commissions are all part of gross pay.

questions.intro: A pre-tax deduction is taken out before income tax is figured, which lowers taxable wages. A traditional 401(k) contribution is pre-tax for income tax, but Social Security and Medicare taxes still apply to it.
questions.question:
Pay stub (biweekly): Gross pay $1,200.00 | 401(k) contribution (pre-tax) $60.00 | Federal income tax $88.00 | Social Security $74.40 | Medicare $17.40 | State income tax $22.80
The 401(k) contribution is pre-tax for federal income tax. What are Gabriel's federal taxable wages for this paycheck?
questions.feedback: $1,200.00 − $60.00 = $1,140.00 of federal taxable wages.

questions.question:
Pay stub (biweekly): Gross pay $1,200.00 | 401(k) contribution (pre-tax) $60.00 | Federal income tax $88.00 | Social Security $74.40 | Medicare $17.40 | State income tax $22.80
Why are Social Security and Medicare figured on $1,200.00, not on $1,140.00 (gross pay minus the pre-tax 401(k) contribution)?

choices.text: 401(k) deferrals are still subject to FICA
The payroll system made an error
FICA taxes are figured on net pay
Social Security is optional for young workers

questions.correct_answer: 401(k) deferrals are still subject to FICA

misconceptions.C: Confuses the FICA base with net pay

questions.feedback: 401(k) deferrals reduce income-taxable wages but not the wages used for Social Security and Medicare.

questions.intro: Because pre-tax contributions lower taxable income, they also lower income tax. Contributing $60 pre-tax reduces take-home pay by less than $60.
questions.question: Gabriel's federal tax rate on his last dollars of income is 12%. If he contributes $60 pre-tax, about how much does his take-home pay drop?
questions.feedback: Tax saved: $60 × 0.12 = $7.20. Take-home drops by $60 − $7.20 = $52.80 (before any state tax effect).

questions.intro: After-tax deductions are taken out after income tax is figured. Roth retirement contributions are after-tax: no tax break now, but qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.
questions.question: A Roth 401(k) contribution is an after-tax deduction. Compared with a traditional (pre-tax) 401(k) contribution of the same amount today, it…

choices.text: lowers today's take-home pay more, but qualified withdrawals later are tax-free
lowers today's take-home pay less and is taxed again later
has no effect on take-home pay
is not allowed for workers under 25

questions.correct_answer: lowers today's take-home pay more, but qualified withdrawals later are tax-free
questions.feedback: Roth contributions do not reduce taxable income now, so take-home falls by the full amount; qualified withdrawals later are tax-free.

questions.question: Which deduction is usually AFTER-tax?

choices.text: A health insurance premium through a cafeteria plan
A health savings account (HSA) payroll contribution

questions.correct_answer: Union dues taken from pay
questions.feedback: Union dues are typically after-tax. Traditional 401(k), cafeteria-plan health premiums, and HSA payroll contributions are typically pre-tax.

questions.intro: Each January, employers send Form W-2, which reports the year's wages and taxes withheld. Its totals should match your last pay stub of the year (for wages subject to each tax).
questions.question: At the end of the year, which form should match the totals on Gabriel's final pay stub?
questions.correct_answer: Form W-2

questions.feedback: The W-2 summarizes the same yearly totals shown in the final YTD amounts.

questions.section_skill: Year-to-date totals and checking for errors
questions.question: Why keep pay stubs until you have checked your W-2?

choices.text: Because banks require them to deposit paychecks
Because they can be exchanged for cash
Because the IRS requires mailing them in each year
To confirm the W-2's wages and withholding are correct

questions.feedback: Pay stubs let you verify the W-2 before filing and catch errors early.

questions.set_title: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2

questions.intro: Form W-4 (Employee's Withholding Certificate) tells your employer how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck. You fill it out when you start a job and can update it any time, such as after a second job begins or your situation changes.

To report her yearly wages to the IRS
To sign up for health insurance
To set her federal income tax withholding

misconceptions.B: Confuses the W-4 with the W-2
misconceptions.C: Confuses tax forms with benefit forms

questions.set_title: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2

questions.question: The U.S. income tax is "pay-as-you-go." What does this mean for employees?

questions.set_title: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2
questions.section_skill: Why taxes are withheld from pay
questions.intro: When you file a tax return, you calculate your actual tax for the year and compare it with what was withheld.
questions.question: If too much tax is withheld during the year, what happens after filing a tax return?

choices.text: The extra is added to next year's salary
The employer pays the employee a bonus
The extra is returned as a refund

questions.correct_answer: The extra is returned as a refund

misconceptions.A: Thinks overpayment is kept by the government

questions.feedback: Overpaid tax is refunded after you file.

questions.set_title: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2
questions.section_skill: Why taxes are withheld from pay
questions.question: If too little tax is withheld, what happens?

choices.text: The employee owes the rest when filing

questions.correct_answer: The employee owes the rest when filing

misconceptions.C: Shifts the debt to the employer

questions.feedback: Underpaid tax is owed with the return, sometimes with a penalty if the shortfall is large.

questions.set_title: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2
questions.section_skill: Why taxes are withheld from pay
questions.question: Which document tells the employer how much to withhold?
questions.correct_answer: Form W-4

misconceptions.B: The W-2 reports what was withheld
misconceptions.C: The stub shows withholding but does not set it

questions.feedback: The W-4 sets withholding; the W-2 reports it after the year ends.

questions.set_title: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2
questions.intro: A tax refund is your own overpaid tax coming back. It is not extra income. A large refund means you could have had more in each paycheck during the year.
questions.question: Last year Kayla received a $1,300 refund. What does that tell her?

choices.text: She earned a $1,300 bonus from the IRS
She had $1,300 more withheld than her tax

questions.correct_answer: She had $1,300 more withheld than her tax

misconceptions.A: Treats a refund as free money

questions.feedback: A refund is a return of overpaid tax, not a bonus.

questions.set_title: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2
questions.question: Kayla's $1,300 tax refund came from tax withheld beyond what she owed. If that amount had stayed in her 26 biweekly paychecks instead, about how much more would each paycheck have been?
questions.feedback: $1,300 ÷ 26 = $50 per paycheck.

questions.set_title: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2
questions.intro: The IRS offers a free online Tax Withholding Estimator. Using recent pay stubs, it suggests how to fill out a new W-4 to get closer to the right amount.
questions.question: Which free tool helps workers check whether their withholding is about right?

choices.text: A social media poll of coworkers

questions.correct_answer: The IRS Tax Withholding Estimator
questions.feedback: The IRS estimator uses your pay information to suggest W-4 changes.

questions.set_title: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2
questions.intro: When you have more than one job, each employer's payroll may assume its pay is your only income, so total withholding can fall short. Step 2 of Form W-4 addresses multiple jobs.
questions.question: Kayla starts a second part-time job. Why might her withholding now be too low?

choices.text: Two jobs always get the correct combined withholding automatically
Each employer withholds as if that job were her only income

questions.correct_answer: Each employer withholds as if that job were her only income

misconceptions.A: Thinks withholding adds up correctly automatically

questions.feedback: Each payroll ignores the other job, so combined income can be under-withheld. Updating the W-4 (Step 2) fixes this.

questions.set_title: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2
questions.question: Kayla expects to owe $200 more than will be withheld this year. She has 10 paychecks left. How much extra per paycheck should she request?

misconceptions.D: Puts the whole amount on one paycheck

questions.feedback: $200 ÷ 10 = $20 per paycheck.

questions.set_title: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2
questions.intro: You may claim "exempt" on Form W-4 only if you had no federal income tax liability last year and expect none this year. Exemption affects federal income tax withholding only, not Social Security or Medicare.
questions.question: Under IRS rules, who may claim exemption from federal income tax withholding on Form W-4?

choices.text: Someone who owed no tax last year and expects none this year
Anyone who works part time while attending high school
Anyone who wants a larger paycheck

questions.correct_answer: Someone who owed no tax last year and expects none this year
questions.feedback: Both conditions must be met: no liability last year and none expected this year.
questions.effective_date: IRS Form W-4 rules as of 2026

questions.set_title: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2
questions.question: A student claims exempt on Form W-4, so no federal income tax is withheld, but earns enough to owe tax. What is the likely result?

choices.text: A larger refund when filing next spring
A tax bill when filing, and possibly a penalty

questions.correct_answer: A tax bill when filing, and possibly a penalty

misconceptions.B: Shifts the tax to the employer

questions.feedback: Exempt status stops withholding, not tax. Tax still owed is due with the return.

questions.set_title: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2
questions.question: If a worker claims exempt from federal income tax withholding on Form W-4, which taxes are still withheld?
questions.correct_answer: Social Security and Medicare
questions.feedback: Exempt status applies only to federal income tax withholding; FICA still applies.

questions.set_title: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2
questions.intro: A claim of exemption from withholding expires and must be renewed with a new Form W-4 each year.
questions.question: How long does a claim of exemption on Form W-4 last?

choices.text: One year; a new W-4 is needed to continue it

questions.correct_answer: One year; a new W-4 is needed to continue it
questions.feedback: Exemption must be renewed each year.

questions.set_title: Form W-4, withholding, and Form W-2
questions.question: IRS rules allow claiming exempt only with no income tax liability last year and none expected this year. Jamal earned $3,000 last year and owed no federal income tax. This year he expects to earn $28,000 at a full-time job. Should he claim exempt?

choices.text: Yes, because he owed nothing last year
Yes, because he is a new worker
Yes, so that he can get a bigger refund next spring
No; he expects to owe income tax this year

questions.correct_answer: No; he expects to owe income tax this year

misconceptions.A: Uses only one of the two conditions

questions.feedback: Both conditions must hold. At $28,000 he would expect to owe tax, so exemption is not allowed.

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.section_skill: Value employee benefits and compare job offers by total compensation
questions.intro: Total compensation is everything an employer provides for your work: wages or salary plus benefits. Common benefits include health insurance (the employer often pays part of the cost), retirement plans with matching contributions, paid time off, and sometimes tuition help or transit passes.
questions.question: Which item is an employee BENEFIT rather than wages?

choices.text: Overtime pay at time and a half
A commission on each sale the worker makes
Hourly pay for a Saturday shift

questions.correct_answer: Employer-paid health insurance
questions.feedback: Employer-paid health insurance is a benefit; the other three are forms of pay.

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.section_skill: Value employee benefits and compare job offers by total compensation
questions.intro: Many employers match retirement contributions, for example "50% of what you contribute, up to 6% of pay." The match is extra money for your retirement, but you only receive it if you contribute.
questions.question: Zoe earns $50,000. Her employer matches 50% of her 401(k) contributions, up to 6% of salary. Zoe contributes 6% ($3,000). How much does the employer add?

misconceptions.D: Gives the total of both contributions

questions.feedback: Zoe contributes $3,000; the employer adds 50% of that: $1,500.

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.section_skill: Value employee benefits and compare job offers by total compensation
questions.question: Zoe's coworker earns $50,000 under the same match (50% of contributions, up to 6% of salary) but contributes only 2% ($1,000). How much potential match does the coworker give up each year?

misconceptions.A: Gives the match received instead of the match missed

questions.feedback: Full match possible: 50% × $3,000 = $1,500. Match received: 50% × $1,000 = $500. Missed: $1,000.

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.section_skill: Value employee benefits and compare job offers by total compensation
questions.intro: To compare offers fairly, subtract the costs you would pay (such as your share of health premiums) and add the value of benefits you would receive (such as a retirement match).
questions.question: Offer A: $48,000 salary; the employee pays $100 per month for health insurance. Offer B: $50,000; the employee pays $250 per month for the same coverage. After subtracting health premiums, which pays more per year, and by how much?
questions.correct_answer: Offer B, by $200

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.section_skill: Value employee benefits and compare job offers by total compensation
questions.question: A job gives 10 paid vacation days. Lin earns $200 per day. What is the dollar value of that paid time off?

misconceptions.D: Thinks paid time off has no value

questions.feedback: Paid time off is pay for days not worked: 10 × $200 = $2,000.

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.intro: Compensation is everything you receive for work. Wages are the pay; benefits are the extras, such as health insurance, retirement contributions, and paid time off, which have real dollar value.
questions.question: What does "total compensation" include?

choices.text: Only the hourly wage or salary
Only the take-home pay after taxes
Only bonuses earned at year end
Pay plus the value of benefits

questions.correct_answer: Pay plus the value of benefits
questions.feedback: Total compensation = pay + benefits.

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.intro: Paid time off means days you are paid for even though you do not work, such as vacation, sick days, or holidays.
questions.question: Which choice is paid time off (PTO)?

choices.text: A lunch break you are not paid for

questions.correct_answer: Paid vacation days
questions.feedback: Paid vacation days are paid time off.

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.question: An employer pays $400 per month toward an employee's health insurance. What is that worth per year?
questions.feedback: $400 × 12 = $4,800 of value per year.

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.intro: A 401(k) is a retirement savings plan offered by many private employers. Workers contribute part of each paycheck, often with tax benefits, and some employers add a match. (Public schools and many nonprofits offer a similar 403(b).)
questions.question: What is a 401(k)?

choices.text: A type of bank checking account for paying monthly bills
A form used to apply for a job
A retirement savings plan offered through an employer

questions.correct_answer: A retirement savings plan offered through an employer
questions.feedback: A 401(k) is an employer-sponsored retirement savings plan.

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.question: Two jobs pay the same salary. Job X offers health insurance; Job Y does not, so the worker must buy coverage for $300 a month. How much more does Job Y effectively cost the worker per year?

misconceptions.A: Ignores the cost of buying coverage

questions.feedback: $300 × 12 = $3,600 a year that Job X's benefit would have covered.

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.intro: A fair comparison adds the value of benefits you will actually use and subtracts costs you will actually pay. A match counts only if you contribute enough to earn it.
questions.question:
Offer C: $52,000 salary, no retirement match, employee health premium $150 per month.
Offer D: $50,000 salary, 401(k) match worth $2,000 per year if you contribute, employee health premium $100 per month.
If you contribute enough to get the full match, which offer is worth more per year, and by how much?
questions.correct_answer: Offer D, by $600

misconceptions.D: Adds the premium difference the wrong way

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.intro: Vesting is ownership over time. Your own 401(k) contributions are always yours. An employer's contributions may vest gradually, and if you leave before you are fully vested, you can lose the unvested part.
questions.question: A 401(k) match "vests" over 3 years. Ali leaves after 1 year. What does vesting mean for him?

choices.text: He may forfeit the unvested part of the employer's match
He loses his own contributions as well as the match
He keeps everything because matches always vest at once

questions.correct_answer: He may forfeit the unvested part of the employer's match

misconceptions.B: Thinks his own money can be forfeited

questions.feedback: Unvested employer money can be forfeited; employee contributions are always 100% vested.

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.question: Under a plan where the match vests 20% per year of service, how much of a $1,500 match has Ali earned after 1 year?

misconceptions.A: Assumes nothing vests in year one

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.question: Which benefit is easiest to overlook when comparing jobs?
questions.correct_answer: A tuition assistance program
questions.feedback: Benefits such as tuition help can be worth thousands of dollars if you will use them.

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.intro: Researching typical income and benefits before choosing a career or job helps you negotiate and plan. The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes pay data and job outlooks by occupation; job postings show current offers.
questions.question: Which source is MOST reliable for typical pay and benefits in an occupation?

choices.text: Government labor data and job postings
A single viral social media post about a high salary
An advertisement for a training course

questions.correct_answer: Government labor data and job postings
questions.feedback: Official labor statistics and actual postings give the most reliable picture.

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.section_skill: The hidden costs of a job
questions.intro: A job's real value can depend on costs it creates: commuting (fuel, parking, transit), uniforms, tools, or child care. Subtracting them gives a clearer comparison.
questions.question: Job E pays $20 per hour, 40 hours a week. The commute costs $12 per day for 5 days. What is the weekly pay after commuting costs?
questions.feedback: Pay: $800. Commute: 5 × $12 = $60. After commuting: $740.

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.section_skill: The hidden costs of a job
questions.question: Job E pays $740 a week after $60 of commuting costs, for 40 hours of work. The commute also takes 1 unpaid hour each day, 5 days a week. Counting commute time, what are the weekly earnings after commuting costs per hour of time spent (work + commute)?
questions.feedback: Time: 40 + 5 = 45 hours. Earnings after costs: $740. $740 ÷ 45 ≈ $16.44 per hour.

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.section_skill: The hidden costs of a job
questions.question: Job E pays $20 per hour, but commuting costs $12 a day for 5 days. Job F pays $19 per hour, fully remote, with no commuting costs. Which earns more per week for 40 hours of work, after commuting costs?
questions.correct_answer: Job F, by $20
questions.feedback: Job F: 40 × $19 = $760 with no costs, which beats Job E's $740 after commuting by $20.

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.section_skill: The hidden costs of a job
questions.question: Which cost should be subtracted when comparing two jobs?

choices.text: Required uniforms the worker must buy
Groceries the worker would buy anyway
Rent the worker pays either way
A phone bill the worker pays either way

questions.correct_answer: Required uniforms the worker must buy
questions.feedback: Subtract costs the job causes, not costs you would have anyway.

questions.set_title: Employee benefits and comparing job offers
questions.section_skill: The hidden costs of a job
questions.question: A parent compares a $22 per hour job requiring $160 per week of child care with an $18 per hour job with a work-site child care benefit (no cost). For 40 hours, which leaves more per week after child care, and by how much?
questions.correct_answer: Neither; both leave $720

questions.section_skill: Compare employee and independent contractor work and estimate gig income after expenses and taxes
questions.intro: An independent contractor works for himself or herself, not as an employee. Payers usually do not withhold taxes, overtime laws generally do not apply, and there are usually no employer benefits. Contractors may receive a Form 1099-NEC (or a 1099-K from a payment platform) instead of a W-2.
questions.question: Ravi drives for a delivery app as an independent contractor. Which statement is TRUE for him but NOT for a typical employee?

choices.text: No taxes are withheld from his pay; he must pay them himself
He is guaranteed overtime pay after 40 hours
His employer pays half of his Social Security tax
He receives a Form W-2 each January

questions.correct_answer: No taxes are withheld from his pay; he must pay them himself
questions.feedback: Contractors receive no withholding; they make their own tax payments, including self-employment tax.

questions.section_skill: Compare employee and independent contractor work and estimate gig income after expenses and taxes
questions.intro: For self-employed work, net earnings (profit) = income − business expenses. Taxes are figured on net earnings, so tracking expenses matters.
questions.question: Ravi earned $900 in delivery fees this month and spent $180 on gas and other business expenses. What were his net earnings?

questions.section_skill: Compare employee and independent contractor work and estimate gig income after expenses and taxes
questions.intro: Self-employment tax is the self-employed person's Social Security and Medicare tax. Because there is no employer to pay half, the rate is 15.3% (12.4% + 2.9%), figured on 92.35% of net earnings. It applies in addition to income tax.
questions.question: Self-employment tax is 15.3% of 92.35% of net earnings. Estimate Ravi's self-employment tax on $720 of net earnings (to the nearest cent).

misconceptions.C: Applies 15.3% to all of the net earnings

questions.section_skill: Compare employee and independent contractor work and estimate gig income after expenses and taxes
questions.intro: Federal income tax applies to income from all sources unless a specific rule excludes it. Forms such as the 1099 report income to the IRS, but they do not decide whether income is taxable.
questions.question: Ravi receives no Form 1099 from one small client who paid him $350. Is the $350 taxable?

choices.text: No; income without a form is tax-free
Only if the client reports it first
Only if the total from that client is over $10,000
Yes; income is taxable even without a form

questions.correct_answer: Yes; income is taxable even without a form

misconceptions.A: Thinks tax depends on a form

questions.feedback: All income is reportable whether or not a 1099 is received. Keeping your own records ensures you report it correctly.

questions.section_skill: Compare employee and independent contractor work and estimate gig income after expenses and taxes
questions.subtopic: Benefits and costs of gig work
questions.question: Which is a benefit of gig work compared with a typical job, and which is a cost?

choices.text: Benefit: guaranteed minimum hours. Cost: fixed schedule
Benefit: employer health insurance. Cost: overtime pay
Benefit: no taxes owed. Cost: lower pay
Benefit: flexibility. Cost: no benefits or withholding

questions.correct_answer: Benefit: flexibility. Cost: no benefits or withholding

misconceptions.A: Describes the opposite of gig work

questions.feedback: Gig work offers flexibility but usually no benefits, no withholding, and uneven income (12-11a).

questions.intro: Employees usually work under an employer's control (schedule, methods) and get a W-2. Independent contractors run their own work, often for several clients, and are paid per job.
questions.question: Which worker is MOST likely an independent contractor?

choices.text: A freelance designer who bills several clients
A cashier scheduled by a store manager each week
A teacher paid a salary by a school district
A warehouse worker paid hourly with a W-2

questions.correct_answer: A freelance designer who bills several clients
questions.feedback: Setting her own hours and billing multiple clients are signs of contractor work.

questions.intro: Businesses that pay a contractor may report the payments on Form 1099-NEC. Payment apps and platforms may send Form 1099-K.
questions.question: Which form might a contractor receive instead of a W-2?
questions.correct_answer: Form 1099-NEC

misconceptions.B: Employees use this to set withholding
misconceptions.D: Used to pay estimated taxes, not received from clients

questions.feedback: Contractors may receive Form 1099-NEC (or 1099-K).

questions.intro: Employers withhold income tax from employees' paychecks. Clients generally pay independent contractors the full amount billed.
questions.question: Who withholds income tax from an independent contractor's pay?

choices.text: The client, just as an employer would for a worker
The bank where the money is deposited
Usually no one; the contractor pays it

questions.correct_answer: Usually no one; the contractor pays it
questions.feedback: Contractors are responsible for paying their own taxes, often through quarterly estimated payments.

questions.intro: Profit (net earnings) = income − expenses.
questions.question: A contractor earns $1,000 and has $250 of business expenses. What is her profit?
Which benefit do contractors usually NOT receive from a client?

choices.text: Control over how they do the work

questions.correct_answer: Employer-paid health insurance
questions.feedback: Employer benefits usually go to employees, not contractors.

questions.intro: Gig apps show gross pay per trip. Your real hourly earnings subtract the costs of doing the work, such as fuel, vehicle wear, phone data, and insurance, then divide by all hours worked, including waiting time.
questions.question: Mia drove 30 hours and earned $750 in app payments. She drove 400 miles, and her costs (gas, wear, insurance) are about $0.30 per mile. What were her earnings per hour after these costs?
A platform takes a 25% service fee from each $40 job. How much does the worker receive per job?
questions.feedback: Fee: $40 × 0.25 = $10. Worker keeps $30.

questions.question: Mia earns $630 a week after driving costs for 30 hours of driving, and she also waits 10 unpaid hours a week for orders. What is her net pay per hour of total time?
questions.feedback: $630 ÷ 40 hours = $15.75 per hour.

questions.question: Mia earns $630 a week after driving costs and sets aside 25% of it for taxes. How much does she keep for the week?

misconceptions.C: Takes 25% of $750 from $750 and ignores costs

questions.question: Which comparison is fair when deciding between gig driving and a $17 per hour employee job?

choices.text: Gig gross per trip vs the job's hourly wage
The busiest gig hour vs the job's average hour
Gig tips only vs the job's full pay
Gig net per hour after costs and taxes vs the job's pay after taxes

questions.correct_answer: Gig net per hour after costs and taxes vs the job's pay after taxes

misconceptions.A: Compares gross gig pay with wages

questions.feedback: Compare like with like: net after all costs and taxes, per hour of time actually spent.

questions.section_skill: Records and taxes for gig workers
questions.intro: Self-employed workers can deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses, such as business miles driven. The IRS expects records that support each deduction: logs, receipts, and statements.
questions.question: Which record is MOST useful for a delivery driver at tax time?

choices.text: A mileage log with dates, miles, and business purpose
A list of restaurants visited for personal meals

questions.correct_answer: A mileage log with dates, miles, and business purpose
questions.feedback: A contemporaneous mileage log supports a vehicle expense deduction.

questions.section_skill: Records and taxes for gig workers
questions.intro: Self-employment tax (Social Security and Medicare for self-employed people) applies once net self-employment earnings reach a small threshold set by law, even if no income tax is owed.
questions.question: Self-employed people generally must file a federal return if net self-employment earnings reach what amount?
questions.feedback: Net self-employment earnings of $400 or more require filing, because self-employment tax applies.

questions.section_skill: Records and taxes for gig workers
questions.intro: Taxes are pay-as-you-go. People without withholding usually make quarterly estimated tax payments (Form 1040-ES) if they expect to owe $1,000 or more. Paying too little during the year can bring a penalty.
questions.question: A gig worker expects to owe $2,000 in tax for the year and pays nothing until April. What risk does this create?

choices.text: No risk; all taxes are due in April
Her tax refund will be larger than usual
An underpayment penalty, plus one large bill

questions.correct_answer: An underpayment penalty, plus one large bill
questions.feedback: Without withholding or estimated payments, she may owe an underpayment penalty.

questions.section_skill: Records and taxes for gig workers
questions.question: Mia sets aside 25% of each week's $630 net in a separate savings account. How much is set aside over a 13-week quarter?

misconceptions.D: Gives total net for the quarter

questions.section_skill: Records and taxes for gig workers
questions.question: Why keep gig tax money in a separate account?

choices.text: So it is not spent before taxes are due
Because the IRS requires a separate account by law
Because separate accounts earn no interest
Because keeping it separate lowers the tax owed

questions.correct_answer: So it is not spent before taxes are due
questions.feedback: Separating tax money protects it from everyday spending.

questions.section_skill: Evaluate how education, skills, and the labor market affect lifetime income
questions.intro: Human capital is the knowledge, skills, and experience that make a person productive and able to earn income. Education, training, apprenticeships, and work experience build human capital, often raising future earnings.
questions.question: Which is an example of investing in your "human capital"?
questions.correct_answer: Completing an electrician apprenticeship
questions.feedback: An apprenticeship builds skills that raise earning power: human capital.

questions.section_skill: Evaluate how education, skills, and the labor market affect lifetime income
questions.intro: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best choice you give up. The cost of school includes tuition and also the income you could have earned while studying.
questions.question: Pat can work now at $32,000 per year, or attend a 4-year program first. What is the opportunity cost in earnings of the 4 years in school (ignoring raises)?
questions.feedback: $32,000 × 4 = $128,000 of earnings given up.

questions.section_skill: Evaluate how education, skills, and the labor market affect lifetime income
questions.intro: Comparing career paths over many years shows the trade-off: a later start can be outweighed by higher yearly earnings, depending on the numbers and costs.
questions.question: Path A: start work at 18 earning $32,000 a year. Path B: start at 22 earning $52,000 a year. Ignoring raises and costs, which path has earned more by age 40, and by how much?
questions.correct_answer: Path B, by $232,000

questions.section_skill: Evaluate how education, skills, and the labor market affect lifetime income
questions.intro: Wages are influenced by supply and demand in the labor market. When employers need more workers with a skill than are available, wages for that skill tend to rise. When many people have a skill employers need less, wages tend to fall.
questions.question: Demand for wind turbine technicians rises sharply, but few people have the training. What usually happens to their wages?
questions.correct_answer: Wages tend to rise

misconceptions.B: Thinks wages are set by law

questions.feedback: High demand and limited supply of a skill push wages up (12-5a).

questions.section_skill: Evaluate how education, skills, and the labor market affect lifetime income
questions.question: Software that automates routine bookkeeping becomes common. Which outcome is MOST likely?

choices.text: Fewer routine jobs, more need for analysis skills
All accounting jobs disappear within a single year
No effect on jobs, because technology never changes work
Higher pay for every routine data-entry job

questions.correct_answer: Fewer routine jobs, more need for analysis skills
questions.feedback: Technology often replaces routine tasks and raises demand for workers who can use the tools and do analysis (12-5b).

questions.intro: Every choice has an opportunity cost: the value of the next-best option you give up. A "free" activity can still cost the money or time you could have used otherwise.
questions.question: Lia can work a Saturday shift for $120 or go to a free concert. If she goes to the concert, what is the opportunity cost?

choices.text: The price of a ticket she did not buy

questions.correct_answer: The $120 she would have earned

misconceptions.C: Confuses the choice with what is given up

questions.feedback: She gives up $120 of pay, the next-best option.

questions.question: Which is the opportunity cost of spending $50 on a video game?

choices.text: What else the $50 could have done
The time it takes to drive to the store

questions.correct_answer: What else the $50 could have done

misconceptions.B: Part of cost but not the main idea here

questions.feedback: Money spent one way cannot be used for the next-best alternative.

questions.intro: Specialized skills take time and money to gain, so fewer people have them. When employers need those skills, they compete for workers by offering higher pay.
questions.question: Why do many careers that require more training pay more?

choices.text: The law requires higher pay for degrees
Training programs set the wages their graduates earn
The skills are scarce and valued

questions.correct_answer: The skills are scarce and valued
questions.feedback: Scarce, valuable skills tend to earn higher wages.

questions.question: Earning $15 per hour for 2 hours vs studying for 2 hours: what is the cost of studying, in income?
questions.feedback: 2 × $15 = $30 of income given up.

questions.question: Which choice is MOST likely to raise long-term earning power?

choices.text: Earning an industry certification in a growing field
Switching to a new phone plan

questions.correct_answer: Earning an industry certification in a growing field
questions.feedback: Certifications build human capital in demand.

questions.section_skill: When does more education pay off?
questions.intro: A "break-even point" is when two options have produced the same total. Write each option's total as an expression in t (years), set them equal, and solve.
questions.question: Path A earns $32,000 a year starting now. Path B costs $40,000 for a 4-year program, then earns $52,000 a year. Let t = years from now (t ≥ 4). Which equation finds when their total earnings (B net of the program cost) are equal?
