questions.question: Mo budgets $1,500 a month and saves any income above that in a buffer account. In a $2,600 month, how much goes to his buffer account?
Mo budgets $1,500 a month and keeps extra income from good months in a buffer account. In a $1,200 month, what should he do?
questions.correct_answer: Draw $300 from his buffer account
questions.feedback: The buffer exists to cover low months: $1,500 − $1,200 = $300.

questions.intro: Some workers with uneven income deposit all earnings into one account and transfer a fixed amount to their spending account each month, like a salary.
questions.question: Which practice makes uneven income easier to manage?

choices.text: Spending each paycheck as soon as it arrives
Budgeting from your single best month
Paying yourself a steady "salary" from a holding account

questions.correct_answer: Paying yourself a steady "salary" from a holding account
questions.feedback: A steady transfer smooths uneven income into predictable spending money.

questions.intro: Many services offer a discount for paying a year at once. Compare by finding the yearly cost of the monthly plan. But a yearly plan only saves money if you would have kept the service all year.
questions.question: A streaming service costs $15.99 per month or $159.99 per year. How much does the yearly plan save compared with paying monthly for 12 months?

misconceptions.D: Subtracts the monthly price from the yearly price
misconceptions.B: Subtracts dollar amounts digit by digit

questions.question: Gina usually cancels streaming services after about 6 months. For her, which plan is cheaper: 6 months at $15.99, or the $159.99 yearly plan?
questions.correct_answer: Monthly: about $95.94

misconceptions.A: Assumes she keeps it all year

questions.question: A gym offers $40 per month with no contract, or $360 for a full year paid up front. After how many months does the yearly plan become the better deal?
questions.correct_answer: More than 9 months

misconceptions.C: Thinks the yearly plan never wins

questions.feedback: $360 ÷ $40 = 9. If she uses the gym more than 9 months, the yearly plan saves money.

questions.question: Which is a risk of a large annual prepayment?

choices.text: Paying for months you may not use

questions.correct_answer: Paying for months you may not use
questions.feedback: Prepaying locks money into a service you might stop using; check the refund policy.

questions.question: A $12.99 monthly subscription renews automatically. Over 3 years, how much does it cost if never cancelled?

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Compare prices using unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.intro: A unit price is the price per unit, such as per ounce or per item: unit price = price ÷ quantity. Comparing unit prices shows which size is the better value. (A lower unit price helps only if you will use the larger amount before it spoils.)
questions.question: A 12-ounce box of cereal costs $3.60. A 20-ounce box costs $5.40. Which is the better buy per ounce?

choices.text: The 12-ounce box, because it costs less

questions.correct_answer: The 20-ounce box: $0.27 per ounce

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Compare prices using unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.intro: A discount is a percent taken off the price. Discount = price × rate. Sale price = price − discount, or price × (1 − rate).
questions.question: A $64 backpack is 25% off. What is the sale price?

misconceptions.A: Gives the discount, not the sale price

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Compare prices using unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.intro: Sales tax is calculated by multiplying the taxable price by the tax rate. Total cost = price + tax, or price × (1 + rate). Rates differ by state and sometimes by city, and some items are exempt.
questions.question: A taxable purchase costs $80. The sales tax rate is 6.5%. What is the TOTAL cost?

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Compare prices using unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.intro: When a discount and a tax both apply, the discount is taken first, and tax is then figured on the sale price.
questions.question: A $120 jacket is 30% off, and the 6.5% sales tax is applied to the sale price. What is the total cost?

misconceptions.D: Applies tax to the original price and adds it to the sale price

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Compare prices using unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.question: A store offers "Buy one, get one 50% off" on $20 shirts. If Tom buys two, what percent does he save on the pair?

misconceptions.A: Uses the dollar amount as a percent

questions.feedback: Two shirts: $20 + $10 = $30 instead of $40. Savings $10 ÷ $40 = 25%.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.intro: A discount lowers the price: sale price = original price − discount.
questions.question: A $50 item has a $10 discount. What is the sale price?

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.intro: Sales tax raises the total: total = price + tax.
questions.question: The tax on a $40 item is $2.60. What is the total?

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.question: Which word describes the percent taken OFF a price?
questions.correct_answer: Discount

misconceptions.D: Interest is a borrowing or saving cost

questions.feedback: A discount reduces the price.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.intro: 10% of an amount is the amount divided by 10.
questions.question: What is 10% of $35?

misconceptions.C: Gives the price after the discount

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.question: Which comparison tells you the better buy between two package sizes?

choices.text: Which package is cheaper in total
Price per ounce of each package

questions.correct_answer: Price per ounce of each package

misconceptions.A: Size alone does not give value

questions.feedback: Unit price compares value across sizes.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.intro: When discounts "stack," each is applied to the price left after the previous one. Two discounts of 20% and 10% do not equal 30% off.
questions.question: A $100 coat is 20% off, with an extra 10% off the sale price at checkout. What is the final price before tax?

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.question: What single percent discount is the same as 20% off followed by 10% off?

misconceptions.A: Multiplies the percents as whole numbers

questions.feedback: Final price is 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72 of the original, so the discount is 28%.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.question: A $5-off coupon and a 15% discount can be used in either order on a $40 purchase. Which order gives the lower price?
questions.correct_answer: 15% first, then $5 off: $29.00

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.question: An ad says "Up to 70% off!" What does this usually mean?

choices.text: Only some items are 70% off; many are discounted less
Every item is at least 70% off

questions.correct_answer: Only some items are 70% off; many are discounted less
questions.feedback: "Up to" sets the maximum discount, not the typical one.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.question: An item's price was $80 last week and is now "on sale" for $80 after being raised to $100 and marked 20% off. What happened?

choices.text: The "sale" price is the same as last week's price
Tom saves $20 compared with last week
Tom saves 20% compared with last week

questions.correct_answer: The "sale" price is the same as last week's price
questions.feedback: $100 × 0.80 = $80, the same as before. Compare with past prices, not just the "was" price.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Total cost beyond the price tag
questions.intro: Compare total cost: price + shipping + fees + tax. A lower sticker price can cost more in total.
questions.question: Store A sells headphones for $59 plus $8 shipping. Store B sells them for $64 with free shipping. Which costs less, and by how much?
questions.correct_answer: Store B, by $3

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Total cost beyond the price tag
questions.question: A store offers free shipping on orders of $50 or more. Jen's cart totals $42, and shipping is $7. She adds a $10 item she does not need. What did that cost her compared with paying shipping?
questions.correct_answer: $3 more
questions.feedback: Paying shipping: $49. Adding the item: $52. She spends $3 more, on something she does not need.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Total cost beyond the price tag
questions.intro: Sales tax rules are set by each state. Some items, such as groceries, clothing, or medicine, may be exempt. Always check your own state's rules.
questions.question: In New Jersey, most clothing and most grocery food are exempt from sales tax, and the general rate is 6.625%. What is the tax on a $40 shirt and a $40 desk lamp bought together?
questions.feedback: The shirt is exempt; the lamp is taxable: $40 × 0.06625 = $2.65.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Total cost beyond the price tag
questions.question: Which purchase decision considers the total cost of owning an item?

choices.text: Choosing the printer with the lowest sticker price only
Choosing the printer with the most colors on the box
Comparing printers by price plus yearly ink costs
Choosing the printer the store displays first

questions.correct_answer: Comparing printers by price plus yearly ink costs
questions.feedback: Ongoing costs (ink, fuel, subscriptions, repairs) can matter more than the purchase price.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Total cost beyond the price tag
questions.question: Printer X costs $60 and $80 a year in ink. Printer Y costs $150 and $35 a year in ink. Over 3 years, which costs less in total?

choices.text: They cost the same over 3 years

questions.correct_answer: Printer Y: $255 vs $300

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices
questions.intro: Every spending choice has an opportunity cost: the next-best thing you give up. Thinking about what else money could do helps you choose deliberately rather than automatically.
questions.question: Kai has $200. He can buy a game console accessory or save toward a used bike. If he buys the accessory, what is the opportunity cost?

choices.text: The $200 price of the accessory itself, paid at the register
Nothing, because he still has the accessory
The sales tax on the accessory
The progress toward the bike that he gives up

questions.correct_answer: The progress toward the bike that he gives up

misconceptions.A: Confuses price with what is given up

questions.feedback: Choosing the accessory means giving up progress toward the bike, the next-best option.

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices
questions.intro: Anchoring is relying too much on the first number you see. A high "original" price can make a sale price feel cheap, even when it is not a good deal compared with other options.
questions.question: A sign says "Was $200, now $120!" Mia feels the $120 price is a great deal, even though similar items cost $100 elsewhere. Which bias is at work?

choices.text: Sunk cost thinking about money already spent
Loss aversion about a past investment loss
The bandwagon effect from friends' choices

questions.correct_answer: Anchoring on the "was" price
questions.feedback: The $200 anchor makes $120 seem cheap; comparing with $100 elsewhere shows it is not.

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices
questions.intro: A sunk cost is money already spent that cannot be recovered. The sunk cost fallacy is letting it drive a new decision. Good decisions compare the future benefits and costs of each option.
questions.question: Leo paid $60 for a concert ticket but feels sick on the day. He goes anyway "so the money isn't wasted." What is this called?
questions.correct_answer: The sunk cost fallacy
questions.feedback: The $60 is gone either way; the choice should depend on how he feels and what he gains now.

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices
questions.intro: Present bias is valuing what we want now much more than what we want later. Impulse buying feeds on it. Adding a delay, such as a 24-hour rule or removing saved cards, gives the planning part of the brain time to weigh in.
questions.question: Ana often buys things online late at night and regrets them. Which strategy targets this habit directly?

choices.text: Save her card details on every site so checkout is faster
Wait 24 hours before buying anything not planned

questions.correct_answer: Wait 24 hours before buying anything not planned
questions.feedback: A waiting period interrupts impulse buying and lets her compare the purchase with her goals.

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices
questions.question: Which ordering follows a sound decision process?

choices.text: Choose quickly, then find reasons to justify the choice later
List options, choose the most popular, skip review
Set a goal, list options, compare, choose, review

questions.correct_answer: Set a goal, list options, compare, choose, review
questions.feedback: A deliberate process defines the goal and compares options before choosing, then reviews the result.

questions.section_skill: Making a choice: alternatives and criteria
questions.intro: Every decision has alternatives (the options) and criteria (what matters to you, such as price, quality, or coverage). Good choices compare alternatives using your criteria.
questions.question: Sam is choosing a phone plan. What are "alternatives"?

choices.text: The different plans he could choose
The reasons he wants a phone
The bill he paid last month

questions.correct_answer: The different plans he could choose
questions.feedback: Alternatives are the options he is choosing among.

questions.section_skill: Making a choice: alternatives and criteria
questions.intro: A criterion (plural: criteria) is a standard you use to judge options, such as cost, quality, or features that matter to you.
questions.question: Which is a CRITERION for choosing a phone plan?
questions.correct_answer: Monthly price
questions.feedback: Price, data, and coverage are criteria that matter for the choice.

questions.section_skill: Making a choice: alternatives and criteria
questions.question: Plan A: $35, 5 GB. Plan B: $45, unlimited. Sam uses about 3 GB a month. Which plan fits his criteria of low cost and enough data?

choices.text: Plan B, because unlimited always sounds better
Plan B, because it costs more

questions.correct_answer: Plan A
questions.feedback: Plan A covers his 3 GB for $10 less per month.

questions.section_skill: Making a choice: alternatives and criteria
questions.question: Plan A costs $35 a month and Plan B costs $45 a month. What is the yearly savings from choosing Plan A?

questions.section_skill: Making a choice: alternatives and criteria
questions.question: After choosing, why review the decision a month later?

choices.text: Because reviewing a purchase lowers its price later
To check whether the choice worked as expected

questions.correct_answer: To check whether the choice worked as expected
questions.feedback: Reviewing lets you learn and adjust future choices.

questions.intro: Scarcity and urgency messages ("only a few left," countdown timers) push quick decisions. Sometimes they are true, sometimes not. Slowing down protects your budget.
questions.question: A website shows "Only 2 left!" and a countdown timer. What is the intended effect?

choices.text: Helping the buyer compare options calmly
Rushing the buyer before comparing options
Showing the store's full inventory honestly

questions.correct_answer: Rushing the buyer before comparing options
questions.feedback: Urgency cues are designed to cut comparison short.

questions.question: A "free trial" requires a card and converts to $14.99 a month unless cancelled. What should Nia do before signing up?

choices.text: Assume it will cancel itself automatically
Set a reminder to cancel before the trial ends
Ignore the terms, since the trial is advertised as free

questions.correct_answer: Set a reminder to cancel before the trial ends
questions.feedback: Free trials often become paid subscriptions automatically; a reminder prevents unwanted charges.

questions.question: A store's loyalty program gives 5% back in points. Raj spends $200 more than he planned to earn points. What did he gain compared with not overspending?

choices.text: He spent $190 more, net of $10 in points

questions.correct_answer: He spent $190 more, net of $10 in points
questions.feedback: 5% of $200 = $10 in points, but he spent $200 extra: a net cost of $190.

questions.intro: "Dark patterns" are design tricks that steer people into choices they did not intend, such as hidden fees, pre-checked add-ons, or hard-to-find cancellation steps.
questions.question: Which design choice is a "dark pattern" that makes spending easier than intended?

choices.text: Making cancellation much harder than signing up
Showing the total price before checkout
Listing all fees clearly up front

questions.correct_answer: Making cancellation much harder than signing up
questions.feedback: Easy sign-up and hard cancellation is a common dark pattern.

questions.question: At checkout, a $4.99 "protection plan" box is already checked on Ben's $25 order. What should he do?

choices.text: Leave it, since stores must check what customers need
Pay it, because it is under $5
Uncheck it unless he decided he wants it

questions.correct_answer: Uncheck it unless he decided he wants it

misconceptions.B: Ignores that it is 20% of the order

questions.feedback: Pre-checked add-ons rely on default bias; $4.99 is about 20% of a $25 order.

questions.intro: Influencers are often paid to promote products and may earn money from each sale. Federal rules require disclosure of these relationships, but the incentive still shapes the message.
questions.question: An influencer promotes a product with a discount code. Which fact matters MOST?

choices.text: The influencer may be paid for each sale
The video looks professional and well produced
The product is popular this week

questions.correct_answer: The influencer may be paid for each sale
questions.feedback: A paid relationship is a reason to compare reviews and prices independently.

questions.question: Friends spend $80 on a dinner out each weekend. Tara's budget allows $30. Which choice best balances friendship and her budget?

choices.text: Join every time and put the extra on a credit card
Join for a lower-cost part or suggest a cheaper place
Cut her rent payment to afford it

questions.correct_answer: Join for a lower-cost part or suggest a cheaper place
questions.feedback: Adapting the plan keeps both the friendships and the budget.

questions.question: Seeing friends' purchases online makes Eli feel he must buy similar things. What is this effect sometimes called?

choices.text: Social comparison, or "keeping up with the Joneses"

questions.correct_answer: Social comparison, or "keeping up with the Joneses"
questions.feedback: Comparing ourselves with others can push spending beyond our plans.

questions.question: Which statement about money and values is MOST accurate?

choices.text: More spending always leads to more happiness over time
Values have no effect on financial choices
Spending that matches your priorities satisfies more
Everyone should have the same priorities

questions.correct_answer: Spending that matches your priorities satisfies more
questions.feedback: Aligning spending with personal priorities, not others' expectations, improves satisfaction.

questions.question: Tara writes her top three money priorities and checks big purchases against them. What does this help with?

choices.text: Making choices that match her goals

questions.correct_answer: Making choices that match her goals
questions.feedback: Written priorities act as criteria for decisions.

questions.section_skill: Set specific savings goals and calculate the time or monthly amount needed to reach them
questions.intro: Effective goals are often written as SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. "Save $1,200 for a laptop by June" names the amount, the purpose, and the deadline, so progress can be tracked.
questions.question: Which savings goal is the most SPECIFIC and measurable?

choices.text: Save more money this year than I did last year
Become better at saving at some point soon
Try to stop spending so much on everything
Save $1,200 for a used laptop by next June

questions.correct_answer: Save $1,200 for a used laptop by next June

misconceptions.C: Not a savings goal with an amount

questions.feedback: It states an amount, a purpose, and a date.

questions.section_skill: Set specific savings goals and calculate the time or monthly amount needed to reach them
questions.intro: Ignoring interest: months needed = goal ÷ monthly saving. Monthly saving needed = goal ÷ months available.
questions.question: Dina saves $150 a month toward an $1,800 goal, starting from $0. How many months will it take (ignoring interest)?
questions.correct_answer: 12 months

questions.section_skill: Set specific savings goals and calculate the time or monthly amount needed to reach them
questions.question: Raul wants $2,400 for a car down payment in 16 months. How much must he save each month (ignoring interest)?

questions.section_skill: Set specific savings goals and calculate the time or monthly amount needed to reach them
questions.intro: If you have a starting amount, subtract it first: monthly saving = (goal − amount saved) ÷ months. This is the equation p·m + start = goal solved for p.
questions.question: Raul wants $2,400 for a car down payment in 16 months and already has $600 saved. How much must he save each month?

questions.section_skill: Set specific savings goals and calculate the time or monthly amount needed to reach them
questions.question: Which goal is LONG-TERM?

choices.text: Saving for a concert ticket next month
Saving for a phone in six months
Saving for a prom outfit this spring

questions.correct_answer: Saving for retirement in 40 years
questions.feedback: Long-term goals are many years away; short-term goals are within about a year.

questions.intro: Saving means not spending part of your income now so you can use it later, for a goal, an emergency, or the future.
questions.question: What is saving?

choices.text: Setting aside income now to use later
Spending money as soon as it is earned
Borrowing money to buy something now

questions.correct_answer: Setting aside income now to use later
questions.feedback: Saving keeps part of today's income for later.

questions.question: Which is a GOOD reason to save?

choices.text: To make your current paycheck larger
To avoid ever needing a budget
To lower your tax rate this year
To pay for a known future expense without borrowing

questions.correct_answer: To pay for a known future expense without borrowing
questions.feedback: Saving lets you pay for goals without debt.

questions.question: Kim saves $20 a week for 10 weeks. How much has she saved?
Kim wants $300 and saves $20 a week. How many weeks will it take?
questions.correct_answer: 15 weeks

questions.question: Which habit makes saving most consistent?

choices.text: Saving only when there is money left over at month end
Saving only in months with birthdays
Waiting until earning a higher salary
Saving a set amount each payday

questions.correct_answer: Saving a set amount each payday
questions.feedback: A set amount each payday turns saving into a routine.

questions.section_skill: Goals with a starting balance and a deadline
questions.intro: A savings plan with a starting amount is linear: total = start + (monthly amount × months). Set the total equal to the goal and solve.
questions.question: Lia has $350 and saves $65 a month. Which equation finds the months m until she has $1,000?

misconceptions.B: Swaps the rate and the start
misconceptions.D: Adds the start to the goal

questions.feedback: Start $350 + $65 per month × m = $1,000.

questions.section_skill: Goals with a starting balance and a deadline
questions.question: Solve 350 + 65m = 1,000. After how many whole months will Lia reach at least $1,000?
questions.correct_answer: 10 months

misconceptions.B: Rounds down; she is still short

questions.feedback: 65m = 650, so m = 10 months.

questions.section_skill: Goals with a starting balance and a deadline
questions.question: Lia has $350 and wants $1,000 in 8 months. How much must she save per month (nearest dollar, rounding up)?
questions.feedback: ($1,000 − $350) ÷ 8 = $81.25, so about $82 a month to be sure.

questions.section_skill: Goals with a starting balance and a deadline
questions.question: Sam's goal: $3,000 in 2 years. He has $600 and can save $90 a month. Will he make it?

choices.text: No; he will have $2,760, which is $240 short

questions.correct_answer: No; he will have $2,760, which is $240 short

questions.section_skill: Goals with a starting balance and a deadline
questions.question: How much more per month would Sam need to close a $240 gap over 24 months?

misconceptions.D: Puts it all in one month

questions.feedback: $240 ÷ 24 = $10 more per month ($100 total).

questions.intro: When there are several goals, rank them by importance and timing, then divide monthly savings among them. Emergency savings usually come first because they protect every other goal.
questions.question: Ray can save $200 a month. Goals: emergency fund (most important), a $600 trip in 6 months, and a car in 3 years. Which plan best reflects his priorities?

choices.text: $200 to the trip only, then everything else
$200 to the car only for 3 years

questions.correct_answer: $100 emergency fund, $100 trip, car later
questions.feedback: $100 × 6 = $600 covers the trip on time while still building the emergency fund.

questions.question: After the trip, Ray sends $150 a month to his car fund. How much will he have after 30 months?
Why keep separate "buckets" or accounts for different goals?

choices.text: Separate accounts always earn more interest
Banks require one account per goal
It shows progress on each goal and avoids spending one goal's money on another

questions.correct_answer: It shows progress on each goal and avoids spending one goal's money on another
questions.feedback: Labeling money by goal keeps plans clear.

questions.question: Ray's goals, in priority order, are an emergency fund, a trip, and a car. He gets a $300 birthday gift. Which use matches his priorities?

choices.text: Spend it all on wants right away
Add it to the car goal only
Leave it in his wallet for months
Add it to the emergency fund first

questions.correct_answer: Add it to the emergency fund first
questions.feedback: Unexpected money can speed up the highest-priority goal.

questions.question: Ray saves for several goals ranked by importance. If his income drops, which goal should he pause first?

choices.text: The least important, least urgent goal

questions.correct_answer: The least important, least urgent goal

misconceptions.D: Rent is a need, not a goal

questions.feedback: Pausing lower-priority goals protects the most important ones.

questions.section_skill: Size, build, and use an emergency fund
questions.intro: An emergency fund is money saved for unexpected events: a lost job, a medical bill, a car repair. It helps you avoid high-cost borrowing when surprises happen. A common guideline is 3 to 6 months of essential expenses, built up gradually. Even a small fund helps.
questions.question: What is an emergency fund for?

choices.text: Planned purchases such as a vacation next summer
Investing in stocks for the highest return
Unexpected costs such as a car repair or a job loss
Paying for holiday gifts each December

questions.correct_answer: Unexpected costs such as a car repair or a job loss

misconceptions.D: Predictable expense; belongs in a sinking fund

questions.feedback: Emergency funds cover unplanned needs; planned goals and investing belong elsewhere.

questions.section_skill: Size, build, and use an emergency fund
questions.question: Jo's essential expenses are $1,650 a month. What is a 3-month emergency fund target?

questions.section_skill: Size, build, and use an emergency fund
questions.intro: Emergency money must be safe and available quickly. Insured savings accounts keep the money stable and accessible. Investments can lose value right when you need them, and long-term CDs charge penalties for early withdrawal.
questions.question: Where is the best place to keep an emergency fund?

choices.text: A stock fund, because it grows faster on average
A 5-year CD with a large early-withdrawal penalty
An insured savings account she can reach quickly
Cash in a drawer at home

questions.correct_answer: An insured savings account she can reach quickly

misconceptions.D: Risk of theft or loss; no interest

questions.feedback: Safety and quick access matter most for emergency money.

questions.section_skill: Size, build, and use an emergency fund
questions.question: Which situation is an appropriate use of an emergency fund?

choices.text: Replacing a broken refrigerator needed for food
A sale on concert tickets that ends tonight
A new phone because a friend got one

questions.correct_answer: Replacing a broken refrigerator needed for food
questions.feedback: An essential, unexpected need is a true emergency.

questions.section_skill: Size, build, and use an emergency fund
questions.question: Jo has $3,000 saved and essential expenses of $1,200 a month. How many months could the fund cover?
questions.correct_answer: 2.5 months

questions.intro: Expected expenses are known in advance (rent, bills, registration). Unexpected expenses are surprises (repairs, medical costs, job loss).
questions.question: Which expense is UNEXPECTED?

choices.text: A dentist visit for a cracked tooth

questions.correct_answer: A dentist visit for a cracked tooth
questions.feedback: A cracked tooth is a surprise expense.

questions.question: How is an emergency fund different from a sinking fund?

choices.text: It is for unknown surprises, not a known future bill
It is for vacations instead of bills

questions.correct_answer: It is for unknown surprises, not a known future bill
questions.feedback: Emergency funds handle surprises; sinking funds handle known costs.

questions.question: Without savings, how do many people pay for a surprise $500 bill?

choices.text: By getting a free refund from the government
By skipping it with no consequence
With money that appears in their account
By borrowing, often at high cost

questions.correct_answer: By borrowing, often at high cost
questions.feedback: No savings often means credit cards, payday loans, or late fees.

questions.question: Paying a $500 repair with a credit card at 24% APR and taking a year to pay it off can cost about how much in interest (rough estimate, half the balance outstanding on average)?

misconceptions.D: Charges interest on the full balance all year

questions.feedback: Average balance ≈ $250; $250 × 0.24 = $60. An emergency fund avoids this cost.

questions.question: Which is a reasonable FIRST emergency-fund target for a teen with a part-time job?

choices.text: Six months of a full adult household's expenses

questions.correct_answer: A starter amount such as $500
questions.feedback: Starting small builds the habit; the target grows with responsibilities.

questions.question: Jo saves $275 a month toward a $4,950 target, starting from $0. How many months will it take?
questions.correct_answer: 18 months

questions.question: Jo's emergency fund target is $4,950. She starts with a $1,500 tax refund and saves $275 a month. How many months of saving does she need (rounded up)?
questions.correct_answer: 13 months

questions.question: Jo used $800 from her emergency fund for a car repair. What should she do next?

choices.text: Borrow $800 to refill it at once
Rebuild the fund with regular deposits

questions.correct_answer: Rebuild the fund with regular deposits
questions.feedback: Rebuilding restores protection for the next surprise.

questions.question: Which automatic setup best builds an emergency fund?

choices.text: A recurring transfer on payday to a separate savings account
Keeping the fund in checking with everyday money
Moving money only when she remembers
Linking the fund to a debit card for shopping

questions.correct_answer: A recurring transfer on payday to a separate savings account
questions.feedback: Automatic transfers to a separate account build the fund consistently.

questions.question: Jo's fund earns 4% a year. If it stays near $4,950 for a year, about how much interest does it earn?
questions.feedback: $4,950 × 0.04 = $198. Safety, not return, is the main job, but interest still helps.

questions.intro: High-interest debt grows quickly, but with no savings at all, the next surprise goes back on the card. A common approach: keep a small starter emergency fund, then put extra money toward high-interest debt, then build the full fund.
questions.question: Kyle has $1,000 saved and a $2,000 credit card balance at 24% APR. Many planners suggest which approach?

choices.text: Spend the $1,000 on wants, then pay minimums
Never pay the card until the fund reaches six months
Keep a small starter fund while paying down the card aggressively
Close the savings account and stop saving

questions.correct_answer: Keep a small starter fund while paying down the card aggressively
questions.feedback: A starter fund prevents new debt while extra payments shrink costly debt.

questions.question: Interest on $2,000 at 24% for one year (simple estimate) is how much?
Savings earn 4% while the card charges 24%. Moving $500 from savings to the card saves about how much per year in net interest?
questions.feedback: Card interest avoided: $500 × 0.24 = $120. Savings interest lost: $500 × 0.04 = $20. Net: $100.

questions.question: Why might someone still keep a few hundred dollars in savings while paying debt?

choices.text: Because savings accounts require it by law
Because card interest stops when you have savings
So a small surprise does not go back on the card
Because debt does not cost anything

questions.correct_answer: So a small surprise does not go back on the card
questions.feedback: A small cushion breaks the cycle of new debt.

questions.question: Kyle has paid off his credit card, which had taken $150 a month in payments. His emergency fund is still small. What is a sensible next step?

choices.text: Increase spending by the payment amount
Send the former card payments to build the full emergency fund

questions.correct_answer: Send the former card payments to build the full emergency fund
questions.feedback: Redirecting the payment amount builds savings quickly.

questions.section_skill: Calculate simple interest and the resulting balance
questions.intro: Simple interest is calculated using I = Prt, where P is the principal (the starting amount), r is the annual interest rate written as a decimal, and t is the time in years.
questions.question: A savings account contains $2,400 and earns 5% simple annual interest. How much INTEREST will the account earn over three years?

misconceptions.A: Calculates one year of interest only
misconceptions.C: Adds one year of interest to the principal
misconceptions.D: Uses an incorrect rate or multiplication

questions.section_skill: Calculate simple interest and the resulting balance
questions.intro: Interest is only the amount earned. The balance is the principal plus the interest: A = P + I.
questions.question: A savings account starts with $2,400 and earns 5% simple annual interest for 3 years. What is the BALANCE at the end?

misconceptions.A: Gives the interest, not the balance
misconceptions.C: Adds only one year of interest

questions.section_skill: Calculate simple interest and the resulting balance
questions.intro: Time in I = Prt must be in years. Convert months to years by dividing by 12: 6 months = 0.5 year.
questions.question: $1,800 earns 4% simple interest for 6 months. How much interest is earned?

questions.section_skill: Calculate simple interest and the resulting balance
questions.intro: Solve I = Prt for the rate: r = I ÷ (P × t). Then write the decimal as a percent.
questions.question: $5,000 earned $600 of simple interest in 3 years. What was the annual rate?

misconceptions.C: Forgets to divide by the years

questions.section_skill: Calculate simple interest and the resulting balance
questions.question: In I = Prt, which quantity is the principal for a $1,500 deposit that earns $90 of interest?
questions.feedback: The principal is the starting amount, $1,500. The interest is $90, and the balance is $1,590.

questions.intro: The principal is the original amount deposited or borrowed. Interest is the extra money earned (or charged). The balance is principal plus interest.
questions.question: Ana deposits $300. A year later she has $309. Which amount is the PRINCIPAL?
questions.feedback: The principal is the original $300.

questions.question: Ana deposits $300, and a year later she has $309. How much INTEREST did she earn?

Which word describes the amount owed or saved after interest is added?
questions.correct_answer: Balance
questions.feedback: The balance is the total after interest.

questions.intro: For a borrower, interest is the cost of using the lender's money. Total repaid = principal + interest.
questions.question: Leo borrows $1,000 and repays $1,080. What was the cost of borrowing?
questions.correct_answer: $80 of interest

questions.section_skill: Solving the interest formula for any variable
questions.intro: The formula I = Prt can be solved for any variable: P = I ÷ (rt), r = I ÷ (Pt), t = I ÷ (Pr).
questions.question: How much must be deposited at 5% simple interest to earn $200 in 2 years?

questions.section_skill: Solving the interest formula for any variable
questions.question: How long will it take $3,000 at 6% simple interest to earn $450?
questions.correct_answer: 2.5 years

questions.question: Which rearrangement of I = Prt correctly gives t?
questions.correct_answer: t = I / (Pr)
questions.feedback: Divide both sides by Pr: t = I / (Pr).

questions.section_skill: Solving the interest formula for any variable
questions.question: $4,000 at 3.5% simple interest earns how much in 18 months?

questions.section_skill: Solving the interest formula for any variable

questions.intro: Some loans charge simple interest on the original principal. For borrowers, I = Prt is the cost of the loan.
questions.question: A friend's family business offers Tim a $1,200 loan at 6% simple interest for 2 years. How much interest will Tim pay?
Tim owes $1,344 in total ($1,200 borrowed plus $144 interest). If he repays it in 24 equal monthly payments, what is each payment?

questions.correct_answer: Loan A, by $15

questions.question: Why do lenders charge interest?

choices.text: To be paid for lending money and taking the risk of not being repaid
Because the law requires every loan to charge 10%
Because money loses value only for lenders

questions.correct_answer: To be paid for lending money and taking the risk of not being repaid
questions.feedback: Interest compensates lenders for the use of their money, for inflation, and for default risk.

questions.question: Which borrower is likely to be offered a LOWER interest rate?

choices.text: One who has missed several payments
One who applies for many loans at once
One with no income to repay
One with a strong record of repaying debts on time

questions.section_skill: Calculate compound interest and compare it with simple interest
questions.intro: When interest is compounded annually, interest is calculated on the current balance, including previously earned interest. For a constant annual rate, A = P(1 + r)^t.
questions.question: $1,000 earns 10% annually, compounded once per year. Assuming the rate stays constant and there are no deposits or withdrawals, what is the balance after two years?

misconceptions.A: Applies one year of interest only

questions.section_skill: Calculate compound interest and compare it with simple interest
questions.intro: With compounding, each year's interest is figured on the balance at the start of that year. Year 1 interest is added to the principal, so year 2 interest is larger.
questions.question: $500 is deposited at 4% interest compounded annually. How much interest is earned in the SECOND year?

misconceptions.A: Uses simple interest on the original $500
misconceptions.C: Gives total interest for two years
misconceptions.D: Gives the balance after two years

questions.section_skill: Calculate compound interest and compare it with simple interest
questions.intro: Simple interest is figured only on the principal: I = Prt. Compound interest is figured on the growing balance: A = P(1 + r)^t, and interest = A − P. The gap between them grows over time.
questions.question: $5,000 earns 4% per year for 3 years. How much MORE interest does annual compounding earn than simple interest?

misconceptions.D: Gives the compound interest, not the difference
misconceptions.B: Gives one year of simple interest

questions.section_skill: Calculate compound interest and compare it with simple interest
questions.intro: To use A = P(1 + r)^t: write the rate as a decimal, add 1, raise to the number of years first (exponents before multiplication), then multiply by P.
questions.question: $2,000 is invested at 6% compounded annually for 10 years. What is the balance (nearest cent)?

questions.section_skill: Calculate compound interest and compare it with simple interest
questions.question: Two accounts both start with $1,000 at 5% for 20 years. One pays simple interest; one compounds annually. Why does the compound account end higher?

choices.text: Its stated rate is really higher than 5%, which the bank does not show
Simple interest accounts charge fees that reduce the balance
It earns interest on earlier interest as well as on the principal
Compounding adds a bonus deposit each year

questions.correct_answer: It earns interest on earlier interest as well as on the principal
questions.feedback: Same rate, same time: compounding wins because interest itself earns interest.

questions.intro: After interest is added, the balance = old balance + interest. That new balance is what earns interest next year when interest compounds.
questions.question: $100 earns 10% interest for one year. What is the balance after one year?

questions.intro: With compound interest, the rate applies to the whole current balance, including interest already earned.
questions.question: The $110 balance earns 10% again in year two. How much interest is earned in year two?

questions.intro: Simple interest: interest on the principal only, the same dollar amount each year. Compound interest: interest on the principal plus accumulated interest, growing each year.
questions.question: Which statement describes COMPOUND interest?

choices.text: Interest is earned only on the original deposit
Interest is paid only when the account is closed
Interest is the same dollar amount every year, figured on the deposit
Interest is earned on the principal and on interest already added

questions.correct_answer: Interest is earned on the principal and on interest already added
questions.feedback: Compound interest earns "interest on interest."

questions.intro: Increasing an amount by r% is the same as multiplying it by (1 + r), with r as a decimal. Adding 5% means multiplying by 1.05.
questions.question: Multiplying by 1.05 is the same as adding what percent?

misconceptions.D: Treats the multiplier as the percent

questions.feedback: × 1.05 = original + 5% of the original.

questions.question: Which expression gives $800 after 3 years at 5% compounded annually?

misconceptions.D: Uses the rate instead of 1 + rate

questions.feedback: Multiply by the growth factor 1.05 once per year: 800(1.05)^3.

questions.intro: In A = P(1 + r)^t, P is the starting amount and (1 + r) is the growth factor per period. A factor of 1.05 means each year's balance is 105% of the year before, a 5% increase.
questions.question: An account balance is modeled by A = 1,500(1.05)^t, where t is years. What does 1.05 tell you?

choices.text: The account pays a $1,500 bonus every 5 years

questions.correct_answer: The balance grows 5% each year

misconceptions.C: Reads the factor as the rate

questions.feedback: 1.05 = 1 + 0.05, so the balance grows 5% per year.

questions.intro: In an exponential model A = P(1 + r)^t, the value when t = 0 is P, because any number raised to the power 0 equals 1.
questions.question: In A = 1,500(1.05)^t, what does 1,500 represent?
questions.correct_answer: The starting balance

misconceptions.B: Confuses the start with a later value

questions.feedback: At t = 0, A = 1,500(1) = 1,500, the starting balance.

questions.question: Using A = 1,500(1.05)^t, what is the balance after 4 years (nearest cent)?
Which model shows a balance that starts at $600 and grows 3% per year?

misconceptions.A: Uses the rate as the factor

questions.feedback: Start 600, growth factor 1 + 0.03 = 1.03.

questions.question: A savings balance doubled from $800 to $1,600 over some years. Which type of growth model fits a fixed annual compound rate?

choices.text: Exponential: the balance multiplies by the same factor each year
Linear: the balance adds the same number of dollars every single year
Quadratic: the balance follows a parabola

questions.correct_answer: Exponential: the balance multiplies by the same factor each year
questions.feedback: Compound interest multiplies by a constant factor each period: exponential growth.

questions.intro: Present value is how much money today grows to a target amount later. Solve A = P(1 + r)^t for P: P = A ÷ (1 + r)^t.
questions.question: Kim wants $10,000 in 5 years. Her account earns 5% compounded annually. How much must she deposit today (nearest cent)?

questions.intro: To find the deposit needed today, divide the future amount by the growth factor raised to the number of years: P = A ÷ (1 + r)^t.
questions.question: Which expression gives the deposit needed today to have $5,000 in 3 years at 4% compounded annually?

misconceptions.C: Uses the rate instead of 1 + rate

questions.feedback: Dividing by (1.04)^3 undoes three years of 4% growth.

questions.intro: Money deposited today earns interest, and the interest compounds, so a smaller amount today can grow into a larger amount later.
questions.question: Why is the deposit needed today SMALLER than the future goal?

choices.text: Banks add a bonus to every goal
Inflation automatically adds extra money to savings accounts each year
Interest will make up the difference over time
The goal amount shrinks every year

questions.correct_answer: Interest will make up the difference over time
questions.feedback: Compound growth turns a smaller deposit into the larger future amount.

questions.intro: In P = A ÷ (1 + r)^t, a higher rate makes the denominator larger.
questions.question: If the rate were higher than 5%, how would the deposit needed today for a $10,000 goal in 5 years change?
questions.correct_answer: It would be smaller
questions.feedback: Faster growth means less money is needed today.

questions.question: Jay can deposit $4,000 today at 6% compounded annually. Will he reach $5,000 within 4 years?

questions.section_skill: Calculate balances with monthly, quarterly, or daily compounding and use APY to compare accounts
questions.intro: When interest compounds n times per year, each period uses the rate r/n, and there are n·t periods: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt). Monthly: n = 12. Quarterly: n = 4. Daily: n = 365.
questions.question: $1,000 is deposited at 6% annual interest compounded monthly. What is the balance after 1 year (nearest cent)?

questions.section_skill: Calculate balances with monthly, quarterly, or daily compounding and use APY to compare accounts
questions.intro: APY (annual percentage yield) is the actual percent growth in one year including compounding: APY = (1 + r/n)^n − 1. Banks must show APY so savers can compare accounts with different compounding.
questions.question: An account pays 6% compounded monthly. What is its APY (nearest hundredth of a percent)?

questions.section_skill: Calculate balances with monthly, quarterly, or daily compounding and use APY to compare accounts
questions.intro: A slightly lower rate compounded more often can produce a higher yield. Compare accounts by APY, not by the stated rate.
questions.question: Account A pays 4.9% compounded daily. Account B pays 5.0% compounded once a year. Which earns more in a year?

choices.text: Account B, because 5.0% is higher than 4.9%
Account B, because daily compounding lowers the yield
Account A: its APY is about 5.02%

questions.correct_answer: Account A: its APY is about 5.02%
questions.feedback: A: (1 + 0.049/365)^365 − 1 ≈ 5.02%. B: 5.00%. Account A earns slightly more.

questions.section_skill: Calculate balances with monthly, quarterly, or daily compounding and use APY to compare accounts
questions.question: $2,000 earns 4% annual interest compounded quarterly for 2 years. What is the balance (nearest cent)?

questions.section_skill: Calculate balances with monthly, quarterly, or daily compounding and use APY to compare accounts

misconceptions.A: Uses the fraction of a year

questions.feedback: Quarterly means 4 times a year, so n = 4.

questions.section_skill: Rates per year and per period
questions.intro: A stated annual rate is split evenly across compounding periods: periodic rate = annual rate ÷ number of periods per year.
questions.question: An annual rate of 6% is compounded monthly. What rate applies each month?
questions.feedback: 6% ÷ 12 = 0.5% per month.

questions.section_skill: Rates per year and per period
questions.intro: Quarterly means four periods per year: periodic rate = annual rate ÷ 4.
questions.question: An annual rate of 8% is compounded quarterly. What is the quarterly rate?
questions.feedback: 8% ÷ 4 = 2% per quarter.

questions.section_skill: Rates per year and per period
questions.intro: Total periods = periods per year × years.
questions.question: How many compounding periods are in 3 years of monthly compounding?

questions.section_skill: Rates per year and per period
questions.intro: To write a percent as a decimal, divide by 100.
questions.question: Write 0.5% as a decimal.

misconceptions.B: Moves the decimal one place too few

questions.section_skill: Rates per year and per period
questions.question: Which compounds MORE often: daily or monthly?
questions.correct_answer: Daily
questions.feedback: Daily = 365 times per year; monthly = 12.

questions.section_skill: How much does compounding frequency matter?
questions.intro: Compounding more often adds a little more interest, because interest starts earning interest sooner. The gain from annual to monthly is noticeable; from monthly to daily it is tiny.
questions.question: $10,000 earns 5% for one year. Compounded annually, the balance is $10,500. Compounded monthly, it is about $10,511.62. Compounded daily, it is about $10,512.67. What pattern do these show?

choices.text: Compounding frequency makes no difference at all to the year-end balance
More frequent compounding helps, but by smaller amounts each step
Monthly compounding earns less than annual

questions.correct_answer: More frequent compounding helps, but by smaller amounts each step
questions.feedback: Annual → monthly adds $11.62; monthly → daily adds only $1.05.

questions.section_skill: How much does compounding frequency matter?
questions.intro: A 1-percentage-point difference in rate changes yearly interest far more than switching between monthly and daily compounding.
questions.question: Comparing savings accounts, which factor usually matters MORE than compounding frequency?

choices.text: Whether interest compounds daily or monthly
The color of the bank's app
The day of the month interest posts

questions.correct_answer: The interest rate itself
questions.feedback: At 5% vs 4%, the rate difference is about $100 a year on $10,000; frequency differences are often a few dollars.

questions.section_skill: How much does compounding frequency matter?
questions.intro: At annual compounding, one year of interest is principal × rate.
questions.question: How much more does $10,000 earn in one year at 5% compounded annually than at 4% compounded annually?

questions.section_skill: How much does compounding frequency matter?
questions.intro: APY already includes the effect of compounding, so the higher APY earns more, whatever the compounding frequency.
questions.question: A bank advertises 4.88% APY compounded daily. Another advertises 4.90% APY compounded monthly. Which pays more?

choices.text: The 4.88% APY account, because daily compounding is better
It cannot be determined from APY

questions.correct_answer: The 4.90% APY account
questions.feedback: APY already includes compounding; 4.90% > 4.88%.

questions.section_skill: How much does compounding frequency matter?
questions.intro: Fees subtract from what an account earns. On small balances, a monthly fee can wipe out most of the interest.
questions.question: An account with a $5 monthly fee pays 4.50% APY. About how much does $2,000 earn in a year after fees?

questions.intro: A promotional ("teaser") rate applies only for a limited time, then drops to the regular rate. Estimate interest for each period separately.
questions.question: A bank offers 5.25% APY for the first 3 months, then the regular 1.00% APY. On $4,000, about how much interest is earned in the first year (simple estimate by period)?

questions.question: Which question should Ana ask about a "limited-time" savings rate?

choices.text: How many people opened accounts today?
What rate applies after the promotion ends?
Will this same rate be offered at every other bank in town?

questions.correct_answer: What rate applies after the promotion ends?
questions.feedback: The post-promotion rate determines long-term earnings.

questions.intro: When a rate changes partway through the year, figure the interest for each part of the year separately.
questions.question: A savings account's variable rate drops from 4% to 3% after six months. On $6,000, about how much interest is earned that year?

questions.intro: Savings rates tend to follow market interest rates, which change with economic conditions and Federal Reserve policy.
questions.question: Why might a bank lower its savings rate?
questions.correct_answer: Market interest rates fell
questions.feedback: Banks adjust variable rates as market rates change.

questions.intro: Most savings accounts have variable rates. A certificate of deposit (CD) usually locks a fixed rate until it matures, in exchange for leaving the money in place.
questions.question: Which product LOCKS a savings rate for a set term?
questions.correct_answer: A certificate of deposit
questions.feedback: CDs usually have a fixed rate for their term.

questions.set_title: Time, doubling, and the Rule of 72
questions.section_skill: Estimate doubling time with the Rule of 72 and explain why starting early matters
questions.intro: The Rule of 72 is a quick estimate: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ (annual interest rate as a percent). It works best for rates between about 4% and 12% and gives an approximation, not an exact answer.
questions.question: Using the Rule of 72, about how long does it take money to double at 6% compounded annually?

misconceptions.A: Uses the rate as the years

questions.set_title: Time, doubling, and the Rule of 72

questions.intro: The Rule of 72 also works backward: rate ≈ 72 ÷ years to double.
questions.question: About what annual rate would double money in 9 years, by the Rule of 72?

misconceptions.C: Uses the years as the rate

questions.set_title: Time, doubling, and the Rule of 72
questions.section_skill: Estimate doubling time with the Rule of 72 and explain why starting early matters
questions.intro: Compound growth speeds up over time because each year's growth is a percent of a larger balance. The last decade can add more than all the earlier decades combined.
questions.question: $5,000 grows at 7% compounded annually. How much MORE does it grow to after 40 years than after 30 years (nearest dollar)?

questions.set_title: Time, doubling, and the Rule of 72

questions.question: Use the Rule of 72 to estimate what $1,000 grows to in 36 years at 8% compounded annually.
questions.correct_answer: About $16,000

questions.set_title: Time, doubling, and the Rule of 72
questions.section_skill: Estimate doubling time with the Rule of 72 and explain why starting early matters
questions.question: Why is the Rule of 72 called an estimate?

choices.text: It only works for simple interest
It approximates the exact compound-interest result
It gives the exact answer for every interest rate and every time period
It is a legal limit on interest rates

questions.correct_answer: It approximates the exact compound-interest result
questions.feedback: It is a shortcut; the exact answer comes from A = P(1 + r)^t.

questions.set_title: Time, doubling, and the Rule of 72
questions.intro: To double means to multiply by 2.
questions.question: $500 doubles once. What is the new amount?

questions.set_title: Time, doubling, and the Rule of 72
questions.intro: Doubling three times multiplies by 2 × 2 × 2 = 2^3 = 8.
questions.question: $500 doubles three times. What is the final amount?

questions.set_title: Time, doubling, and the Rule of 72
questions.intro: Number of doublings = total years ÷ years per doubling.
questions.question: If money doubles every 10 years, how many times does it double in 30 years?
questions.correct_answer: 3 times
questions.feedback: 30 ÷ 10 = 3 doublings.

questions.set_title: Time, doubling, and the Rule of 72
questions.intro: Steady additions grow by the same dollar amount each year (linear growth). Doubling multiplies the amount (exponential growth). Exponential growth starts slowly but eventually passes linear growth.
questions.question: Starting with $100, which is larger after 30 years: adding $100 each year, or doubling every 10 years?
questions.correct_answer: Adding $100 a year: $3,100 vs $800

misconceptions.D: Counts five doublings instead of three

questions.set_title: Time, doubling, and the Rule of 72
questions.question: Which statement about compound growth is TRUE?

choices.text: Growth is fastest in the first year
Growth is the same number of dollars every year
Growth is faster in later years because the balance is larger

questions.correct_answer: Growth is faster in later years because the balance is larger
questions.feedback: Each year adds a percent of a larger balance, so dollar growth speeds up.

questions.set_title: Time, doubling, and the Rule of 72
questions.intro: Starting early gives money more years to compound. Someone who saves for a few early years can end up with more than someone who saves much longer but starts later. (These examples assume a steady 7% return; real investment returns vary and are not guaranteed.)

questions.intro: Compounding rewards time. Money invested earlier has more years for its earnings to earn more.
questions.question: Saver A contributed $20,000 and ended with about $210,000. Saver B contributed $60,000 and ended with about $189,000. Why did A end with more?

choices.text: A's money had more years to compound
A contributed more money in total than B did

questions.set_title: Time, doubling, and the Rule of 72
questions.question: Saver A contributed $20,000 and ended with about $210,000. About how much of A's $210,000 came from growth rather than contributions?

Every year earns exactly 7%, so results are certain
