questions.set_title: Time, doubling, and the Rule of 72
questions.intro: Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ rate. Number of doublings = years invested ÷ years per doubling.
questions.question: $1,000 invested at 6% for 36 years doubles about how many times (Rule of 72)?
questions.correct_answer: 3 times
questions.feedback: 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years per doubling; 36 ÷ 12 = 3 doublings.

questions.set_title: Time, doubling, and the Rule of 72
questions.intro: At a given rate, one fewer doubling period at the end means one fewer doubling: the final balance is about half as large.
questions.question: $1,000 invested at 6% doubles about every 12 years. Waiting 12 years to invest it, with a fixed retirement date, means ending with about…
questions.correct_answer: half as much

misconceptions.D: Uses the years as a percent

questions.feedback: Losing one doubling period cuts the result by about half.

questions.set_title: Time, doubling, and the Rule of 72
questions.question: $1,000 grows at 6% for 36 years to about $8,000. If Jen invests the $1,000 at 6% but waits 12 years, so it grows for 24 years, about how much will she have?
questions.correct_answer: About $4,000

questions.set_title: Time, doubling, and the Rule of 72
questions.intro: Savers cannot control market returns, inflation, or interest rates. They can control when they start, how much they save, and how consistently they save.
questions.question: Which factor does a young saver control MOST?

choices.text: Interest rates set by the Federal Reserve
How early and how consistently they save

questions.correct_answer: How early and how consistently they save
questions.feedback: Time and consistency are within the saver's control.

questions.set_title: Time, doubling, and the Rule of 72
questions.question: Two friends each save $100 a month. One starts at 22, the other at 32. Both stop at 65 and earn the same rate. Which statement is TRUE?

choices.text: The earlier saver will very likely end with much more
They will end with the same amount
The later saver will end with more
Saving monthly removes the effect of starting time completely

questions.correct_answer: The earlier saver will very likely end with much more
questions.feedback: Ten extra years of contributions and compounding produce a much larger balance.

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.section_skill: Choose a savings product by safety, liquidity, and return
questions.intro: A certificate of deposit (CD) is a bank or credit union deposit that you agree to leave for a set term, such as 6 months or 5 years. In return, it usually pays a fixed rate. Taking money out before the term ends usually costs an early-withdrawal penalty. CDs are insured deposits up to the legal limit.
questions.question: What is a certificate of deposit (CD)?

choices.text: A stock that pays the same fixed dividend to owners every month
A checking account with free checks
A deposit left for a set term at a usually fixed rate
A loan that a bank gives to students

questions.correct_answer: A deposit left for a set term at a usually fixed rate

misconceptions.A: Confuses a CD with a stock
misconceptions.D: Confuses a CD with a loan

questions.feedback: A CD is a time deposit with a set term and usually a fixed rate.

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.section_skill: Choose a savings product by safety, liquidity, and return
questions.intro: Early-withdrawal penalties are often stated as a number of days or months of interest. Penalty ≈ principal × rate × (days ÷ 365).
questions.question: Max's $5,000 CD pays 4.5% simple interest. The penalty for early withdrawal is 90 days of interest. About how much is the penalty (use 365 days in a year)?

misconceptions.D: Uses a full year of interest

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.section_skill: Choose a savings product by safety, liquidity, and return
questions.intro: A money market deposit account is a bank deposit, insured up to the legal limit. A money market fund is a mutual fund that invests in short-term debt. It aims to keep a stable value but is not FDIC insured and can, rarely, lose value.
questions.question: Which statement about a money market DEPOSIT account (at a bank) and a money market FUND (at a brokerage) is TRUE?

choices.text: Only the deposit account is FDIC insured
Only the fund is FDIC insured
Neither can ever lose value, because both are offered by banks

questions.correct_answer: Only the deposit account is FDIC insured

misconceptions.A: Thinks the similar names mean the same protection
misconceptions.D: Overstates the safety of the fund

questions.feedback: The bank account is a deposit (insured); the fund is an investment (not FDIC insured).

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.section_skill: Choose a savings product by safety, liquidity, and return
questions.intro: Match the product to when you need the money. Money needed on a known date can go in a CD whose term ends by that date. Money you may need any time belongs in a savings account.
questions.question: Lily will need $3,000 for college fees in exactly 12 months, and she will not touch it before then. Which choice fits best?

choices.text: A 5-year CD with a large early-withdrawal penalty
A stock fund, for the highest possible return
A 12-month CD at an insured bank
Her checking account, which pays no interest

questions.correct_answer: A 12-month CD at an insured bank

misconceptions.B: Value can fall right before she needs it

questions.feedback: A 12-month CD matches the timeline and keeps the money safe.

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.section_skill: Choose a savings product by safety, liquidity, and return
questions.question: Which choice keeps emergency money BOTH safe and quickly available?

choices.text: A 3-year CD that charges an early-withdrawal penalty
A high-yield savings account at an insured bank

questions.correct_answer: A high-yield savings account at an insured bank

misconceptions.B: Hard to sell at a known price

questions.feedback: Insured savings combine safety with quick access (liquidity).

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.section_skill: Liquidity: how quickly money can be used
questions.intro: Liquidity describes how easily and quickly something can be turned into cash you can spend, without losing value. Cash and checking are very liquid; a house is not.
questions.question: What does "liquidity" mean in personal finance?

choices.text: How quickly money can be used without losing value
How much interest an account pays each year, as a percent
How much water a bank uses
How large an account balance is

questions.correct_answer: How quickly money can be used without losing value
questions.feedback: Liquidity = quick access without loss of value.

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.section_skill: Liquidity: how quickly money can be used
questions.intro: Checking account money can be spent today. Selling a house or car, or ending a CD early, takes time or costs money.
questions.question: Which is MOST liquid?
questions.correct_answer: Money in a checking account

misconceptions.D: Takes time to sell; value uncertain

questions.feedback: Checking money is available immediately.

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.section_skill: Liquidity: how quickly money can be used
questions.intro: Savers usually earn more for accepting less liquidity, such as locking money in a CD for a longer term.
questions.question: Why do longer-term CDs often pay higher rates than savings accounts?

choices.text: Banks are required to pay more on CDs by law
You give up access to the money for longer

questions.correct_answer: You give up access to the money for longer
questions.feedback: Less liquidity is usually rewarded with a higher rate.

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.section_skill: Liquidity: how quickly money can be used
questions.question: Which money should be kept the MOST liquid?

choices.text: A college fund for a newborn
Money for a house in 10 years

questions.correct_answer: An emergency fund
questions.feedback: Emergency money must be available on short notice.

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.section_skill: Liquidity: how quickly money can be used
questions.question: A 2-year CD pays 4%; a savings account pays 3.5%. On $1,000 for one year, about how much more does the CD earn?
questions.feedback: $40 − $35 = $5 more, in exchange for less access.

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.intro: A CD ladder spreads money across CDs with different maturity dates. One CD matures each year, giving regular access to part of the money, and maturing CDs can be reinvested at current rates.
questions.question: Rosa splits $4,000 into four CDs of $1,000 each, maturing in 1, 2, 3, and 4 years. What is this strategy called?
questions.correct_answer: A CD ladder
questions.feedback: Staggered maturities form a "ladder."

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.intro: In a CD ladder, one CD (one "rung") matures each year.
questions.question: In a 4-rung ladder of $1,000 CDs maturing in years 1–4, how much becomes available each year?
questions.feedback: One $1,000 CD matures each year (plus its interest).

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.question: Rosa's ladder pays 3.8%, 4.0%, 4.1%, and 4.2% on $1,000 each. What is the total interest in the first year (simple interest)?

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.question: Why might a ladder be better than putting all $4,000 in one 4-year CD?

choices.text: A ladder always pays the highest possible rate on every single dollar
Part of the money becomes available every year without penalty

questions.correct_answer: Part of the money becomes available every year without penalty
questions.feedback: Ladders balance higher long-term rates with yearly access.

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.question: When the 1-year CD matures, rates have risen. What does a typical ladder strategy do?

choices.text: Withdraw it and close the ladder
Reinvest it in a new 4-year CD at the higher rate
Reinvest it for 1 year only, forever
Break the other CDs early so all the money can be reinvested

questions.correct_answer: Reinvest it in a new 4-year CD at the higher rate
questions.feedback: Rolling each maturing CD into the longest rung keeps the ladder going and captures new rates.

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.intro: Treasury bills are short-term loans to the U.S. government. They are sold at a discount, a price below face value, and pay the full face value at maturity. The difference is the earnings. Treasury securities are backed by the U.S. government.
questions.question: A $1,000 Treasury bill (T-bill) is bought for $975 and pays $1,000 when it matures. How much does the buyer earn?

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.intro: The return as a percent of what you paid = earnings ÷ price × 100.
questions.question: A T-bill bought for $975 pays $1,000 at maturity, earning $25. What percent of the purchase price is that (nearest hundredth)?

misconceptions.D: Gives price as a percent of face

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.intro: I bonds are U.S. savings bonds whose rate includes an inflation adjustment that changes every six months. They must be held at least 12 months, and cashing them in before 5 years costs the last 3 months of interest.
questions.question: Series I savings bonds have a rate that adjusts with inflation. What is the main purpose of that feature?

choices.text: To help savings keep up with rising prices
To guarantee the bond doubles in value every single year
To make the bond a stock investment

questions.correct_answer: To help savings keep up with rising prices
questions.feedback: The inflation-adjusted rate helps protect purchasing power.

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.intro: I bond rules: they cannot be cashed during the first 12 months, and cashing them in before 5 years forfeits the last 3 months of interest.
questions.question: Under the rules described for I bonds, what happens if one is cashed after 2 years?

choices.text: Nothing; there is never a penalty
The last 3 months of interest are lost
It cannot be cashed until it reaches its 30-year final maturity

questions.correct_answer: The last 3 months of interest are lost
questions.feedback: Before 5 years, the last 3 months of interest are forfeited.

questions.set_title: Savings options: high-yield savings, CDs, and money market accounts
questions.intro: Individuals can buy Treasury bills, notes, bonds, and savings bonds directly from the U.S. Treasury on its TreasuryDirect website, or through a bank or broker.
questions.question: Where can individuals buy Treasury securities directly from the government?
questions.correct_answer: TreasuryDirect.gov
questions.feedback: TreasuryDirect is the Treasury's official site for buying securities directly.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.section_skill: Explain the parts of a loan and compare secured and unsecured borrowing
questions.intro: Every loan has a principal (the amount borrowed), interest (the cost of borrowing), and a term (how long you have to repay). Total repaid = principal + interest (+ any fees).
questions.question: Lena borrows $6,000 for 3 years and will repay $6,840 in total. Which amount is the PRINCIPAL?

misconceptions.D: Confuses the total repaid with principal

questions.feedback: The principal is the amount borrowed: $6,000. Interest is $840.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.section_skill: Explain the parts of a loan and compare secured and unsecured borrowing
questions.intro: The cost of borrowing is everything you repay beyond the amount you borrowed.
questions.question: For the same kind of loan, Lena borrows $6,000 and repays $6,840 in total over 3 years. What did borrowing cost her?

misconceptions.D: Treats the whole repayment as cost

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.section_skill: Explain the parts of a loan and compare secured and unsecured borrowing
questions.intro: Collateral is property a borrower pledges to a lender. A secured loan is backed by collateral (a car for an auto loan, a home for a mortgage); if the borrower does not repay, the lender can take it. An unsecured loan has no collateral, so lenders usually charge more.
questions.question: Which loan is SECURED?

choices.text: An auto loan where the lender can repossess the car
A credit card with no collateral
A personal loan approved based only on the borrower's income
A student loan with no collateral

questions.correct_answer: An auto loan where the lender can repossess the car
questions.feedback: The car is collateral for an auto loan, so it is secured.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.section_skill: Explain the parts of a loan and compare secured and unsecured borrowing
questions.intro: Interest rates reflect risk. When a lender cannot take property to recover a loan, it faces more risk of loss and usually charges a higher rate.
questions.question: Why do unsecured loans usually have HIGHER interest rates than secured loans?

choices.text: The lender has no collateral to take if unpaid
Secured loans are not regulated, so they can charge anything
Unsecured lenders must pay extra taxes

questions.correct_answer: The lender has no collateral to take if unpaid
questions.feedback: More risk for the lender means a higher rate.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.section_skill: Explain the parts of a loan and compare secured and unsecured borrowing
questions.question: Which choice is generally a BETTER use of borrowing?

choices.text: A loan for a vacation that will be paid off over five years
A cash advance to buy concert tickets
A modest loan for training that raises future earnings
A loan to cover gambling losses

questions.correct_answer: A modest loan for training that raises future earnings

misconceptions.A: Long-term debt for a short-term want
misconceptions.D: Debt that does not create value

questions.feedback: Borrowing that builds income or lasting value can be worthwhile; borrowing for short-lived wants usually costs more than it is worth.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.intro: Principal is the amount borrowed. Interest is the extra amount paid for borrowing. Total repaid = principal + interest.
questions.question: Jay borrows $500 from a credit union and repays $530. Which is the INTEREST?

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.intro: Total repaid = principal + interest.
questions.question: A loan has a principal of $2,000 and total interest of $240. What is the total repaid?

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.intro: The term of a loan is how long the borrower has to repay it, such as 36 months.
questions.question: Which word means "the length of time to repay a loan"?
questions.correct_answer: Term
questions.feedback: The term is the repayment period.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.question: From a BORROWER'S point of view, what is interest?

choices.text: Money the bank pays the borrower each month on the loan
The price paid for using someone else's money

questions.correct_answer: The price paid for using someone else's money
questions.feedback: Borrowers pay interest to lenders.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.question: Two loans of $1,000 have the same term. Loan A costs $90 in interest; Loan B costs $150. Which is cheaper?

choices.text: Loan B, because it charges more interest
They are equal because the principal is the same
It cannot be told without knowing the lenders' names

questions.correct_answer: Loan A
questions.feedback: Same principal and term: lower interest means a cheaper loan.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.intro: A cosigner signs a loan along with the borrower and promises to repay it if the borrower does not. The debt can appear on the cosigner's credit report, and late payments can hurt the cosigner's credit.
questions.question: Maya's older brother asks her to cosign his car loan. What does cosigning mean?

choices.text: Maya is only a reference with no responsibility
Maya becomes the owner of the car
Maya is legally responsible for the debt if he does not pay
Maya pays only if she later signs a second agreement to do so

questions.correct_answer: Maya is legally responsible for the debt if he does not pay
questions.feedback: A cosigner is fully responsible for the debt if the borrower does not pay.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.intro: When a cosigned loan goes unpaid, the lender can collect from the cosigner, and the missed payments can be reported on the cosigner's credit report too.
questions.question: Maya cosigned her brother's car loan. He misses three payments. What can happen to Maya?

choices.text: Her credit can be harmed and the lender can ask her to pay
Nothing happens to her, because the car is in her brother's name
Only her brother's credit is affected

questions.correct_answer: Her credit can be harmed and the lender can ask her to pay
questions.feedback: The cosigner is responsible for payments, and late payments can show up on her credit report.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.intro: Financial counselors suggest cosigning only if you could and would repay the whole loan yourself.
questions.question: Before cosigning, which question is MOST important for Maya to ask herself?

choices.text: Will my brother be grateful to me for helping him out?
Could I afford to make every payment myself?
Is the car a nice color?
Will the dealer give me a gift?

questions.correct_answer: Could I afford to make every payment myself?
questions.feedback: Only cosign a debt you could repay yourself.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.intro: If the borrower stops paying, the lender can collect each scheduled payment from the cosigner.
questions.question: A cosigned $15,000 loan has payments of $300 a month. If the borrower stops paying, how much would the cosigner owe over the next year?

misconceptions.D: Assumes the full balance is due at once

questions.feedback: $300 × 12 = $3,600 in payments for the year.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.question: What is a safer way for Maya to help her brother than cosigning?

choices.text: Lend him her debit card PIN
Cosign two smaller loans for him instead of one large loan
Take out a cash advance for him
Help him build credit or save for a larger down payment

questions.correct_answer: Help him build credit or save for a larger down payment
questions.feedback: Helping him qualify on his own avoids putting her credit at risk.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.intro: One way to judge a loan is to compare its total cost with the benefit it creates, such as higher income.
questions.question: A $3,000 loan for a welding certificate costs $360 in interest. The certificate raises Dan's pay by $4 an hour for 2,000 hours a year. What is the extra pay in the first year?
questions.feedback: $4 × 2,000 = $8,000, far more than the $360 of interest.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.intro: When you borrow to pay for something, its true cost is the price plus the interest and fees.
questions.question: A $2,000 vacation is paid with a 24% loan over 2 years, costing about $540 in interest. What is the trip's total cost?

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.question: Which question best tests whether a purchase should be financed?

choices.text: Is the monthly payment smaller than my current phone bill?
Does the store offer instant approval?
Will it be worth more than its total cost by payoff?
Will my friends think it is cool?

questions.correct_answer: Will it be worth more than its total cost by payoff?
questions.feedback: Comparing lasting value with total cost avoids paying long after the benefit is gone.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.intro: Advertisements often emphasize a low monthly payment. Multiply the payment by the number of payments to find the total.
questions.question: A store says, "Only $49 a month!" for a $1,200 laptop over 36 months. What is the total paid?
questions.feedback: $49 × 36 = $1,764, which is $564 more than the price.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.question: Which is generally the cheapest way to buy a $300 bike you need for work?

choices.text: Saving for it over a few months and paying cash
Rent-to-own at $15 a week for a year
A credit card that is paid off slowly over three years

questions.correct_answer: Saving for it over a few months and paying cash
questions.feedback: Paying cash from savings avoids interest and fees entirely.

questions.section_skill: Interpret APR and convert it to monthly and daily periodic rates
questions.intro: APR (annual percentage rate) is the yearly cost of credit, including the interest rate and certain fees, expressed as a percent. Lenders often charge interest each month using a periodic rate: monthly periodic rate = APR ÷ 12.
questions.question: A loan has an APR of 18%. If interest is charged monthly, what is the monthly periodic rate?

misconceptions.C: Confuses APR with a monthly rate

questions.feedback: 18% ÷ 12 = 1.5% per month.

questions.section_skill: Interpret APR and convert it to monthly and daily periodic rates
questions.intro: Many credit cards use a daily periodic rate = APR ÷ 365 (some use 360). Interest is figured each day on the balance.
questions.question: A credit card has a 21.9% APR and charges interest daily. What is the daily periodic rate (use 365 days; nearest thousandth of a percent)?

misconceptions.D: Confuses APR with a daily rate

questions.section_skill: Interpret APR and convert it to monthly and daily periodic rates
questions.intro: Comparing loans by interest rate alone can mislead, because fees add to the cost. APR includes the interest rate and certain fees, which makes it the better number for comparing loans of the same term.
questions.question: Two $5,000 loans for one year: Loan A has a 9% interest rate plus a $150 fee; Loan B has a 10% interest rate and no fee. Which has the lower total cost?
questions.correct_answer: Loan B: $500 vs $600

questions.section_skill: Interpret APR and convert it to monthly and daily periodic rates
questions.intro: Interest for one period = balance × periodic rate.
questions.question: A $1,200 balance has a monthly periodic rate of 2%. How much interest is charged for one month?

questions.section_skill: Interpret APR and convert it to monthly and daily periodic rates
questions.question: Which statement about APR is TRUE?

choices.text: It is the monthly payment amount
It is set by law, so it is the same at every lender
It is the amount still owed on the loan
It states the yearly cost of credit as a percent

questions.correct_answer: It states the yearly cost of credit as a percent

misconceptions.A: Confuses a rate with a payment
misconceptions.C: Confuses a rate with a balance

questions.feedback: APR expresses the yearly cost of credit, so it helps compare offers.

questions.intro: A year has 12 months. A yearly rate spread evenly across months is the yearly rate ÷ 12.
questions.question: A rate is "per year." How is it changed to a rate "per month"?
questions.correct_answer: Divide by 12
questions.feedback: Yearly ÷ 12 = monthly.

questions.intro: Monthly rate = yearly rate ÷ 12.
questions.question: A rate of 12% per year equals what rate per month?

questions.intro: Simple yearly rate = monthly rate × 12.
questions.question: A monthly rate is 1.5%. What is the equivalent simple yearly rate?

questions.intro: To compare rates, put them in the same time unit first.
questions.question: Which is LARGER: 2% per month or 20% per year?
questions.correct_answer: 2% per month (24% per year)
questions.feedback: 2% × 12 = 24% per year, more than 20%.

questions.intro: APR stands for annual percentage rate.
questions.question: What does the "A" in APR stand for?
questions.correct_answer: Annual
questions.feedback: APR = annual percentage rate.

questions.section_skill: APR versus APY and effective cost
questions.intro: APR is a simple yearly rate: monthly rate × 12. If interest is added each month and then charged interest, the effective annual rate (like APY for savings) is higher: (1 + monthly rate)^12 − 1.
questions.question: A loan charges 1.5% per month, compounded monthly. What is the effective annual rate (nearest tenth of a percent)?

questions.section_skill: APR versus APY and effective cost
questions.intro: For the same compounding, APY (or the effective annual rate) is higher than APR whenever interest compounds more than once a year. Federal rules require savings to show APY and loans to show APR.
questions.question: Savings accounts advertise APY, while loans advertise APR. Why might a lender prefer to advertise APR?

choices.text: APR is always higher than APY
APR leaves out compounding, so it looks lower
APR includes all possible fees, making it look higher
APR is used only for savings

questions.correct_answer: APR leaves out compounding, so it looks lower
questions.feedback: The effective cost with compounding is higher than the stated APR.

questions.section_skill: APR versus APY and effective cost
questions.intro: When interest compounds more than once a year, the effective annual rate is higher than the stated APR.
questions.question: A credit card has a 24% APR with daily compounding. Is the effective annual rate higher or lower than 24%?

choices.text: It depends on the cardholder's name

questions.correct_answer: Higher
questions.feedback: Compounding makes the effective rate a bit above 24% (about 27%).

questions.section_skill: APR versus APY and effective cost
questions.intro: The APR of a loan includes the interest rate and certain fees, so loans with the same term can be compared by APR.
questions.question: Which number should Ali use to compare two personal loans with the same term but different fees?

choices.text: Only the monthly payment, ignoring the term

questions.correct_answer: The APR of each loan
questions.feedback: For loans of the same term, APR captures both rate and certain fees.

questions.section_skill: APR versus APY and effective cost
questions.intro: APR for a simple one-year loan ≈ (interest + fees) ÷ amount borrowed × 100.
questions.question: A $1,000 loan for one year has a $50 fee and charges 5% interest. Roughly what is its APR?

misconceptions.D: Uses the fee as a percent

questions.intro: The Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to show key terms before you sign: the APR, the finance charge (the dollar cost of credit), the amount financed, and the total of payments.
questions.question: A Truth in Lending disclosure shows: Amount financed $8,000; Finance charge $1,620; Total of payments $9,620. What is the finance charge?

choices.text: The full amount of money borrowed: $8,000
The dollar cost of the credit: $1,620

questions.correct_answer: The dollar cost of the credit: $1,620
questions.feedback: The finance charge is the total dollar cost of credit.

questions.intro: When payments are equal, each payment = total of payments ÷ number of payments.
questions.question: The same disclosure: Amount financed $8,000; Total of payments $9,620; 48 monthly payments. What is each payment (nearest cent)?

questions.intro: Comparing the finance charge with the amount financed shows how much the credit costs relative to the amount borrowed.
questions.question: Amount financed $8,000; finance charge $1,620. The finance charge is what percent of the amount financed (nearest tenth)?

misconceptions.B: Divides by the total of payments

questions.feedback: $1,620 ÷ $8,000 = 0.2025 → 20.3% of the amount borrowed, spread over 4 years.

questions.intro: Federal law (the Truth in Lending Act) requires the disclosure so borrowers see the cost of credit in a standard form.
questions.question: Why must lenders give this disclosure BEFORE you sign?

choices.text: So you can compare offers and understand the cost
So the lender can raise the rate later without telling you
Because the IRS requires it for taxes
So you can skip reading the contract

questions.correct_answer: So you can compare offers and understand the cost

questions.section_skill: Calculate debt-to-income ratio and choose a debt repayment strategy
questions.intro: Two common payoff strategies: the avalanche method pays minimums on all debts and puts extra money toward the highest interest rate first (saving the most interest); the snowball method puts extra toward the smallest balance first (quick wins that build motivation).
questions.question: Debts: Card A $1,200 at 24% APR; Card B $400 at 18% APR; Loan C $3,000 at 7% APR. Under the AVALANCHE method, which debt gets extra payments first?
questions.correct_answer: Card A (highest APR)
questions.feedback: Avalanche targets the highest APR: Card A at 24%.

questions.section_skill: Calculate debt-to-income ratio and choose a debt repayment strategy
questions.intro: The snowball method pays minimums on all debts and puts every extra dollar toward the smallest balance first.
questions.question: Using the same three debts (Card A $1,200 at 24%; Card B $400 at 18%; Loan C $3,000 at 7%), which debt does the SNOWBALL method pay off first?
questions.correct_answer: Card B (smallest balance)
questions.feedback: The snowball method pays the smallest balance first: Card B ($400).

questions.section_skill: Calculate debt-to-income ratio and choose a debt repayment strategy
questions.intro: Paying down a higher-rate debt removes more interest each month: interest avoided ≈ amount × (APR ÷ 12).
questions.question: In one month, how much more interest does $200 of extra payment save on a 24% APR card than on a 7% APR loan (monthly rate = APR ÷ 12)?
questions.feedback: Card: $200 × 0.02 = $4.00. Loan: $200 × 0.07 ÷ 12 ≈ $1.17. Difference ≈ $2.83 per month, and it continues every month.

questions.section_skill: Calculate debt-to-income ratio and choose a debt repayment strategy
questions.question: A lender prefers DTI below 36%. Amir earns $4,000 gross monthly and already pays $700 in debts. What is the most in additional monthly debt payments he could take on and stay at or below 36%?

questions.intro: A ratio compares two quantities. Payments to income = payments ÷ income.
questions.question: Monthly debt payments are $500 and income is $2,500. What is the ratio of payments to income, as a fraction in simplest form?

questions.intro: To write a fraction as a percent, divide, then multiply by 100.
questions.question: Write 1/5 as a percent.

questions.intro: Lenders usually calculate DTI with gross (before-tax) monthly income.
questions.question: Which income should be used for DTI as lenders usually figure it?
questions.correct_answer: Gross monthly income
questions.feedback: DTI uses gross monthly income.

questions.intro: DTI counts payments on debts (loans, credit cards, mortgages or rent in some calculations), not everyday expenses like food.
questions.question: Which counts as a monthly DEBT payment for DTI?
questions.correct_answer: A student loan payment
questions.feedback: Loan payments count; everyday expenses usually do not.

questions.question: If DTI goes from 15% to 40%, what has happened?

choices.text: A larger share of income now goes to debt payments
Debt has been paid off, freeing up more of the income

questions.correct_answer: A larger share of income now goes to debt payments
questions.feedback: A higher DTI means more of each dollar is committed to debt.

questions.intro: Sometimes the highest-rate debt is also the smallest balance, so both methods choose the same first target.
questions.question: Lee has $300 a month for debts beyond minimums. Debts: $500 at 22%, $2,000 at 22%, $800 at 10%. Which method choice is the same under both avalanche and snowball for the first target?

choices.text: Both pay the $2,000 debt at 22% first
Both pay the $500 debt at 22% first

questions.correct_answer: Both pay the $500 debt at 22% first
questions.feedback: The $500 debt is the smallest AND tied for the highest rate.

questions.intro: Research on behavior suggests quick wins can help people stick with a plan. The best method is one you will actually follow.
questions.question: Which reason might lead someone to choose the snowball method even though it can cost more interest?

choices.text: It always saves the most interest
It lowers the interest rates on the other debts automatically
Paying off small debts quickly keeps them motivated

questions.correct_answer: Paying off small debts quickly keeps them motivated
questions.feedback: Motivation from early payoffs can matter as much as the math.

questions.intro: The "rollover" step: when one debt is paid off, its payment is added to the next target, so payments grow like a snowball.
questions.question: After Card B ($400) is paid off, Lee rolls its $40 minimum plus his $200 extra into the next debt. How much now goes to the next debt each month beyond its own minimum?

questions.intro: The interest saved by paying one debt instead of another is about the amount × the difference in rates.
questions.question: Two $1,000 debts: one at 25% APR, one at 5% APR. Paying the 25% debt first instead of the 5% debt avoids roughly how much interest per year on that $1,000?

questions.intro: A debt inventory, a list of every debt with its balance, rate, and minimum payment, is the starting point for any payoff plan.
questions.question: Which step should come BEFORE choosing a payoff method?

choices.text: Listing each debt's balance, rate, and minimum
Skipping minimum payments on the smallest debts for a while

questions.correct_answer: Listing each debt's balance, rate, and minimum
questions.feedback: You cannot choose a target without knowing balances, rates, and minimums.

questions.intro: Debt consolidation combines several debts into one new loan, ideally at a lower rate. It can lower interest and simplify payments, but only if the new rate is lower and new debt is not added.
questions.question: Pia combines $6,000 of credit card debt at 23% APR into a personal loan at 11% APR. About how much interest does this save in the first year (simple estimate on the full balance)?

questions.intro: Consolidation moves debt; it does not change spending habits.
questions.question: After consolidating, Pia keeps using her credit cards and builds new balances. What happens?

choices.text: The loan pays the new card debt automatically
Her rate on the cards drops to 11%
She ends up with the loan AND new card debt

questions.correct_answer: She ends up with the loan AND new card debt
questions.feedback: Without changing spending, consolidation can lead to more total debt.

questions.intro: An origination fee is a one-time charge for making a loan, often a percent of the loan amount. It adds to the cost and should be included in comparisons.
questions.question: A consolidation loan has a 5% origination fee on $6,000. How much is the fee?

questions.intro: Debt relief companies that sell services by phone generally cannot charge fees until they actually settle or reduce a debt. Up-front fee demands are a warning sign.
questions.question: Which consolidation offer should raise suspicion?

choices.text: A credit union loan with a stated APR and no prepayment penalty
A bank personal loan with a clear fee schedule
A company that wants large fees up front to "settle" debts
A nonprofit credit counselor offering a free budget review

questions.correct_answer: A company that wants large fees up front to "settle" debts
questions.feedback: Up-front fees for debt settlement are a red flag.

questions.intro: Nonprofit credit counseling agencies can review your budget and debts and may offer debt management plans.
questions.question: Where can someone get free or low-cost help making a debt plan?

choices.text: An anonymous social media account offering tips

questions.correct_answer: A nonprofit credit counseling agency
questions.feedback: Reputable nonprofit credit counselors help with budgets and debt plans.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Explain the consequences of missed payments and the rights of consumers with debt in collection
questions.intro: Missing a payment usually brings a late fee first. Payments 30 or more days late can be reported to credit bureaus and hurt credit scores. Unpaid debts can be sold to collectors, and creditors can sue for unpaid debts.
questions.question: Ana misses a credit card payment by 10 days. Which consequence is MOST likely first?

choices.text: Her wages are garnished the next day
Her bank account is closed by law

questions.correct_answer: A late fee

misconceptions.D: Not a consequence of a late card payment

questions.feedback: A late fee usually comes first; credit reporting generally follows when a payment is 30+ days late.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Explain the consequences of missed payments and the rights of consumers with debt in collection
questions.intro: Under federal law, most negative items stay on credit reports for 7 years. Some bankruptcies can stay for up to 10 years. Positive information can stay longer.
questions.question: Most negative information, such as late payments or collections, can stay on a credit report for about how long?
questions.correct_answer: 7 years
questions.feedback: About 7 years for most negative items; up to 10 years for some bankruptcies.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Explain the consequences of missed payments and the rights of consumers with debt in collection
questions.intro: The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act gives consumers rights: collectors must provide validation information about the debt, consumers can dispute it, and collectors may not harass, threaten, or lie.
questions.question: A debt collector calls about an old debt Sam does not recognize. What right does he have?

choices.text: To have the whole debt erased simply by asking for that
To make the collector pay him for the call
To dispute the debt and receive validation information

questions.correct_answer: To dispute the debt and receive validation information
questions.feedback: He can dispute the debt; the collector must provide information validating it.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Explain the consequences of missed payments and the rights of consumers with debt in collection
questions.intro: Collectors may not threaten arrest or legal action they cannot or do not intend to take.
questions.question: A collector threatens to have Rina arrested over a $400 credit card debt. What is true?

choices.text: She must pay immediately or go to jail
This threat is illegal; debt is not a crime
Collectors may say anything to get paid
Arrest is a normal step for unpaid debts over $300

questions.correct_answer: This threat is illegal; debt is not a crime
questions.feedback: Threatening arrest for ordinary debt is a prohibited practice. She can report it to the CFPB.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Explain the consequences of missed payments and the rights of consumers with debt in collection
questions.intro: Bankruptcy is a federal court process. Chapter 7 can discharge many debts, sometimes after selling some assets; Chapter 13 sets a repayment plan, usually over 3–5 years. Some debts, such as most student loans and child support, are hard or impossible to discharge.
questions.question: What is bankruptcy?

choices.text: A free way to cancel all debts with no consequences
A court process to erase or reorganize debts
A credit card for people with debt

questions.correct_answer: A court process to erase or reorganize debts
questions.feedback: Bankruptcy is a serious legal option of last resort with lasting credit effects.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Due dates, late fees, and minimum payments
questions.intro: A due date is the deadline for a payment. Paying after it can bring a late fee and, if very late, other consequences.
questions.question: A bill says "Due June 15." Ali pays on June 18. What usually happens?

choices.text: He may be charged a late fee
Nothing, because three days is close enough

questions.correct_answer: He may be charged a late fee
questions.feedback: Paying after the due date can trigger a late fee.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Due dates, late fees, and minimum payments
questions.intro: The minimum payment is the smallest amount that keeps an account in good standing that month. It does not pay off the balance.
questions.question: A card's minimum payment is $35 on a $900 balance. If Ali pays $35, what happens to the rest?

choices.text: It is paid by the card company
It must be paid separately in cash at a bank branch
It carries over and can be charged interest

questions.correct_answer: It carries over and can be charged interest
questions.feedback: The remaining $865 carries over, often with interest.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Due dates, late fees, and minimum payments
questions.question: Which habit best prevents missed payments?

choices.text: Paying only when reminded by a collector
Autopay for at least the minimum
Paying whatever is left at month end

questions.correct_answer: Autopay for at least the minimum
questions.feedback: Autopay for at least the minimum, plus extra when possible, prevents late payments.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Due dates, late fees, and minimum payments
questions.intro: Comparing a fee with the payment shows how large it is: fee ÷ payment × 100.
questions.question: A $35 late fee on a $25 minimum payment adds what percent to the amount due that month?

misconceptions.B: Uses the fee as a percent

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Due dates, late fees, and minimum payments
questions.question: If you know you will miss a payment, what should you do first?

choices.text: Ignore all calls and letters until the problem passes
Open a new card to pay it
Contact the lender to ask about options

questions.correct_answer: Contact the lender to ask about options
questions.feedback: Lenders may offer hardship plans or new due dates if contacted early.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: Consumers can tell a debt collector in writing to stop contacting them. The collector may then contact them only to confirm or to say it will take a specific action, such as filing a lawsuit. The debt itself still exists.
questions.question: Sam wants a collector to stop calling. Under federal rules, what can he do?

choices.text: Pay a fee to stop the calls
Ask his bank to block the debt from being collected
Ask in writing that it stop contacting him

questions.correct_answer: Ask in writing that it stop contacting him
questions.feedback: A written request stops most contact, though the debt remains and the collector may still sue.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: After a collector first contacts you, it must send validation information. If you dispute the debt in writing within the validation period (generally 30 days), the collector must pause collection until it verifies the debt.
questions.question: Sam gets a validation notice and believes the amount is wrong. Within how many days of receiving it should he dispute in writing to require the collector to verify the debt before continuing collection?
questions.correct_answer: 30 days
questions.feedback: Dispute in writing within about 30 days of receiving the validation notice.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: Collectors may contact you to collect, but federal law bans harassment, threats, false statements, and unfair practices.
questions.question: Which collector behavior is prohibited?

choices.text: Sending a letter with the amount owed
Calling during normal hours to ask for payment

questions.correct_answer: Calling repeatedly to harass
questions.feedback: Harassment, such as repeated calls meant to annoy, is prohibited.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: The CFPB and state attorneys general accept complaints about debt collection.
questions.question: Where can someone report a collector who breaks the rules?

choices.text: The CFPB or the state attorney general
The collector's own sales and marketing team

questions.correct_answer: The CFPB or the state attorney general
questions.feedback: The CFPB and state attorneys general handle these complaints.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: A settlement is an agreement to pay less than the full balance. Get the terms in writing before paying, and keep proof of payment.
questions.question: A collector offers to settle a $2,000 debt for $1,200. What should Sam get before paying?

choices.text: Nothing; a phone promise is enough
A new credit card from the collector

questions.correct_answer: The settlement agreement in writing
questions.feedback: A written agreement protects against later claims for the rest.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: Most negative items stay on a credit report for 7 years from when the trouble began.
questions.question: Sam's collection account was reported 3 years ago. About how many more years will it typically stay on his credit report?
questions.correct_answer: 4 years
questions.feedback: 7 − 3 = 4 more years (generally measured from the original delinquency).

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: The impact of old negative items fades over time, especially when new on-time payments build a better record.
questions.question: Which action usually helps a credit report recover over time?

choices.text: Opening many new cards at once
Making every new payment on time
Paying a company to erase accurate negatives

questions.correct_answer: Making every new payment on time

misconceptions.D: Accurate information cannot be removed for a fee

questions.feedback: Recent on-time payments gradually outweigh older problems.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: You can dispute inaccurate information for free. Accurate negative information generally stays for the time allowed by law, no matter who you pay.
questions.question: A company promises to remove ACCURATE negative information from a credit report for $500. What should a consumer know?

choices.text: Accurate negatives cannot be removed early
It is the only way to fix credit
The credit bureaus require consumers to buy this service

questions.correct_answer: Accurate negatives cannot be removed early
questions.feedback: Credit repair cannot remove accurate information; disputing errors is free.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: A statute of limitations limits how long a creditor can sue over a debt. It varies by state, and in some states a payment can restart the clock.
questions.question: In some states, making a small payment on a very old debt can do what?

choices.text: Make the debt illegal to collect from that point on
Restart the time limit for a lawsuit on that debt

questions.correct_answer: Restart the time limit for a lawsuit on that debt
questions.feedback: Before paying an old debt, learn your state's rules on the statute of limitations.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: Chapter 13 bankruptcy reorganizes debts: a person with regular income repays creditors through a court-approved plan.
questions.question: Which statement about Chapter 13 bankruptcy is TRUE?

choices.text: It is the same as a debt management plan from a counselor
It sets a court-approved repayment plan, often 3–5 years
It has no effect on credit

questions.correct_answer: It sets a court-approved repayment plan, often 3–5 years
questions.feedback: Chapter 13 reorganizes debts into a repayment plan, usually 3–5 years.

questions.section_skill: Explain how a credit card works: credit limit, revolving balance, and grace period
questions.intro: A credit card lets you borrow up to a credit limit to make purchases. The card issuer pays the store, and you owe the issuer. Each month you get a statement and can pay the full balance or a smaller amount (at least the minimum). Any unpaid balance "revolves" to the next month, usually with interest.
questions.question: Leo uses a credit card to buy a $90 jacket. What happens to his money right away?

choices.text: $90 leaves his checking account immediately, as with a debit card
Nothing yet; he now owes the card issuer $90
The store waits to be paid until Leo pays his bill
The jacket is free if he pays the minimum each month

questions.correct_answer: Nothing yet; he now owes the card issuer $90
questions.feedback: The issuer paid the store; Leo now owes the issuer $90.

questions.section_skill: Explain how a credit card works: credit limit, revolving balance, and grace period
questions.intro: The credit limit is the most you can owe on the card at one time. Available credit = credit limit − current balance.
questions.question: Mia's card has a $1,500 credit limit and a $620 balance. How much more can she charge?

misconceptions.D: Adds the balance to the limit

questions.feedback: $1,500 − $620 = $880 of available credit.

questions.section_skill: Explain how a credit card works: credit limit, revolving balance, and grace period
questions.intro: Most cards have a grace period: if you pay the full statement balance by the due date, you are not charged interest on new purchases. The law requires statements to be sent at least 21 days before the due date. Carrying a balance usually ends the grace period until the card is paid in full again.
questions.question: Ben pays his full statement balance by the due date every month. How much interest does he pay on purchases?

choices.text: The full APR on every purchase
Half the APR, because he pays on time

misconceptions.C: Confuses the minimum payment with interest

questions.feedback: Paying in full by the due date keeps the grace period, so no purchase interest is charged.

questions.section_skill: Explain how a credit card works: credit limit, revolving balance, and grace period
questions.intro: Credit comes in two main forms. Installment credit (car loans, student loans) is one amount repaid in fixed payments. Revolving credit (credit cards, lines of credit) can be used again and again up to a limit, with payments that change with the balance.
questions.question: Which statement describes "revolving" credit?

choices.text: You can borrow, repay, and borrow again up to a limit
You borrow one fixed amount and repay it on a schedule
You can only use it once, then the account closes
The balance is paid automatically by the bank

questions.correct_answer: You can borrow, repay, and borrow again up to a limit
questions.feedback: Credit cards are revolving: available credit returns as you repay.

questions.section_skill: Explain how a credit card works: credit limit, revolving balance, and grace period
questions.intro: The Credit CARD Act of 2009 says applicants under 21 must show independent income or assets to repay, or have a cosigner who is at least 21.
questions.question: Jada is 19 with no income and applies for a credit card on her own. Under federal law, what does she need?

choices.text: Only a school ID, because students get automatic approval
Independent income, or a cosigner 21 or older
Nothing; anyone over 18 must be approved
A parent's permission slip signed at school

questions.correct_answer: Independent income, or a cosigner 21 or older
questions.feedback: Under-21 applicants need their own ability to repay or a cosigner 21 or older.

questions.intro: A debit card takes money from your own account. A credit card borrows money you must repay.
questions.question: With a DEBIT card, where does the money come from?

choices.text: A loan from the card issuer, repaid next month

questions.correct_answer: The cardholder's own bank account
questions.feedback: Debit spends money already in your account.

questions.intro: Every credit card purchase is borrowing. The amount is added to your card balance, which you owe the card issuer.
questions.question: With a CREDIT card, what does the cardholder create with each purchase?

choices.text: A debt owed to the card issuer
A reduction in their bank balance right away

questions.correct_answer: A debt owed to the card issuer
questions.feedback: Each credit purchase adds to what you owe.

questions.intro: A credit limit is a borrowing maximum, not money you own.
questions.question: Sam's credit limit is $2,000. Does that mean he has $2,000 of his own money?

choices.text: Yes; the limit is deposited into his account
No; it is the most he can borrow
No; it is the minimum he must spend

questions.correct_answer: No; it is the most he can borrow
questions.feedback: The limit is borrowing capacity that must be repaid.

questions.intro: Interest is charged on borrowed money that is not repaid on time.
questions.question: Which payment method can lead to paying INTEREST if the bill is not paid in full?
questions.correct_answer: A credit card

misconceptions.A: No interest; it spends your own money

questions.feedback: Unpaid credit card balances can be charged interest.

questions.intro: Federal law caps your liability for unauthorized credit card charges at $50. Debit card limits depend on how fast you report a problem.
questions.question: Which card typically has STRONGER federal protection against unauthorized charges?
questions.correct_answer: A credit card
questions.feedback: Credit cards have a $50 cap; debit card protection depends on how quickly you report.

questions.section_skill: What is APR on a credit card?
questions.intro: A credit card's APR is its yearly interest rate. Interest for about a month ≈ balance × (APR ÷ 12). (Many cards actually figure interest daily.)
questions.question: A card has a 24% purchase APR. If Kai carries a $500 balance for a whole month, about how much interest is charged (monthly rate = APR ÷ 12)?

questions.section_skill: What is APR on a credit card?
questions.intro: Cards can have different APRs for purchases, cash advances, and balance transfers, plus a penalty APR that can apply after a late payment, often 60 days late for existing balances.
questions.question: A card lists several APRs: purchase APR 21.99%, cash advance APR 29.99%, penalty APR 29.99%. When does the PENALTY APR usually apply?

choices.text: On every purchase made on weekends
Only on balance transfers made in the first month
Never; it is only shown for decoration

questions.correct_answer: After a serious late payment
questions.feedback: The penalty APR applies after late payments, as described in the agreement.

questions.section_skill: What is APR on a credit card?
questions.intro: The best card depends on how you use it. If you always pay in full, the APR rarely matters, but fees do.
questions.question: Two cards: Card A 18% APR, $0 annual fee; Card B 15% APR, $95 annual fee. Ana pays in full every month. Which costs her less?

choices.text: Card B, because 15% is lower than 18%
Card B, because annual fees are refunded
Card A, because she never pays interest

questions.correct_answer: Card A, because she never pays interest

misconceptions.A: Ignores that she pays no interest

questions.feedback: Paying in full means no interest, so the $95 fee is the only cost difference.

questions.section_skill: What is APR on a credit card?
questions.intro: Under the Credit CARD Act, issuers generally must give 45 days' notice before a significant change such as a higher APR on new purchases.
questions.question: Card issuers must give advance notice before raising the APR on future purchases. How many days of notice does the law generally require?
questions.correct_answer: 45 days
questions.feedback: Generally 45 days' advance notice.

questions.section_skill: What is APR on a credit card?
questions.intro: Daily interest = balance × (APR ÷ 365).
questions.question: A 24% APR card charges interest daily on a $500 balance. About what is the daily interest (APR ÷ 365)?

questions.intro: A cash advance means using your credit card to get cash (at an ATM or bank). It is borrowing. Cash advances usually have a fee, a higher APR, and no grace period: interest starts right away.
questions.question: A cash advance is…

choices.text: borrowing cash against your credit card
withdrawing your own savings with a debit card
a free bonus paid by the card issuer
a refund of a returned purchase

questions.correct_answer: borrowing cash against your credit card
questions.feedback: A cash advance is a loan of cash from your card issuer.

questions.intro: Cash advance fees are often the larger of a percent of the amount or a minimum dollar amount.
questions.question: Tom takes a $200 cash advance. The fee is 5% (minimum $10). What is the fee?
questions.feedback: 5% of $200 = $10, which equals the $10 minimum, so the fee is $10.

questions.intro: Interest on a cash advance starts the day it is taken. Interest ≈ amount × (APR ÷ 365) × days.
questions.question: A $400 cash advance has a 5% fee and a 29.99% APR with no grace period. About how much interest accrues in 30 days (daily rate = APR ÷ 365)?

questions.intro: The total cost of a cash advance includes both the fee and the interest.
questions.question: Tom's $400 cash advance cost a $20 fee plus about $9.86 of interest after 30 days. What was the total cost?
Which is usually a cheaper way to get $100 cash quickly than a credit card cash advance?

choices.text: Taking a cash advance on two cards instead of one
Withdrawing from your own savings or checking

questions.correct_answer: Withdrawing from your own savings or checking
questions.feedback: Using your own money avoids fees and interest.

questions.section_skill: Read a credit card statement and decide how much to pay and when
questions.intro: A credit card statement lists the previous balance, payments, new purchases, fees, interest, the new (statement) balance, the minimum payment, and the due date. Paying the full statement balance by the due date avoids interest on purchases (the grace period).
questions.question:
Credit card statement (closing date May 20): Previous balance $640.00 | Payments −$640.00 | Purchases +$412.75 | Fees $0.00 | Interest charged $0.00 | New balance $412.75 | Minimum payment due $25.00 | Payment due date June 15 | Purchase APR 22.99%
How much must Rosa pay by June 15 to avoid ANY interest on these purchases?
questions.feedback: Paying the full new balance, $412.75, by June 15 keeps the grace period.

questions.section_skill: Read a credit card statement and decide how much to pay and when
questions.intro: The minimum payment due is the smallest amount that avoids a late fee that month. Paying only the minimum leaves the rest of the balance owed, and interest is charged on it.
questions.question:
Credit card statement (closing date May 20): Previous balance $640.00 | Payments −$640.00 | Purchases +$412.75 | Fees $0.00 | Interest charged $0.00 | New balance $412.75 | Minimum payment due $25.00 | Payment due date June 15 | Purchase APR 22.99%
What is the LEAST Rosa can pay by June 15 and keep her account in good standing?
questions.feedback: The minimum payment due is $25.00; paying only that leaves $387.75 to carry over with interest.

questions.section_skill: Read a credit card statement and decide how much to pay and when
questions.question:
Credit card statement (closing date May 20): Previous balance $640.00 | Payments −$640.00 | Purchases +$412.75 | Fees $0.00 | Interest charged $0.00 | New balance $412.75 | Minimum payment due $25.00 | Payment due date June 15 | Purchase APR 22.99%
If Rosa pays only the $25 minimum, what balance carries into next month before interest?
questions.feedback: $412.75 − $25.00 = $387.75, which will then be charged interest.

questions.section_skill: Read a credit card statement and decide how much to pay and when
questions.intro: When the previous statement balance was paid in full by its due date, new purchases usually get a grace period, so no purchase interest appears on the next statement.
questions.question:
Credit card statement (closing date May 20): Previous balance $640.00 | Payments −$640.00 | Purchases +$412.75 | Fees $0.00 | Interest charged $0.00 | New balance $412.75 | Minimum payment due $25.00 | Payment due date June 15 | Purchase APR 22.99%
The statement shows "Interest charged $0.00." Why?
