questions.question: If Nia pays only $150 a month on the $4,120 during the 15-month 0% period, how much remains when the promotion ends?

questions.set_title: Card fees, balance transfers, and promotional offers
questions.intro: A balance transfer only helps if the debt shrinks. New spending can rebuild the old balance while the transferred one is being paid.
questions.question: Which habit can undo the benefit of a balance transfer?

choices.text: Tracking the date the promotion ends each month
Running up new charges on the old card

questions.correct_answer: Running up new charges on the old card
questions.feedback: New charges can leave two balances instead of one.

questions.set_title: Card fees, balance transfers, and promotional offers
questions.intro: Compare the interest avoided during the promotion with the transfer fee.
questions.question: A transfer offer: 0% for 6 months, 5% fee. Debt: $2,000 at 18% APR. About how much would 6 months at 18% cost (simple), and is the transfer worth it?

choices.text: About $180 in interest vs a $100 fee; worth it if paid off in 6 months

questions.correct_answer: About $180 in interest vs a $100 fee; worth it if paid off in 6 months
questions.feedback: $2,000 × 0.18 × 0.5 = $180 vs 5% × $2,000 = $100: saves about $80, if paid off in time.

questions.set_title: Card fees, balance transfers, and promotional offers
questions.intro: Three numbers decide whether a transfer saves money: the transfer fee, how long the promotional rate lasts, and the rate afterward.
questions.question: Which fact should Nia check BEFORE transferring?

choices.text: The fee, promo length, and later APR

questions.correct_answer: The fee, promo length, and later APR
questions.feedback: Those three numbers decide whether a transfer saves money.

questions.section_skill: Explain what credit reports contain, get free reports, and dispute errors
questions.intro: A credit report is a record of how you have used credit: accounts, balances, payment history, and some collections. Three nationwide credit bureaus (consumer reporting agencies) keep reports: Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion.
questions.question: Which company is one of the three nationwide credit bureaus?
questions.correct_answer: Experian
questions.feedback: Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion are the three nationwide credit bureaus.

questions.section_skill: Explain what credit reports contain, get free reports, and dispute errors
questions.intro: Federal law gives you free credit reports. The official site is AnnualCreditReport.com, where free reports from all three bureaus are available (weekly, under a permanent program).
questions.question: Where can Jordan get free credit reports from all three bureaus?

choices.text: Any website that advertises "free credit score"
The bank where Jordan opened checking

questions.correct_answer: AnnualCreditReport.com
questions.feedback: AnnualCreditReport.com is the official free source.

questions.section_skill: Explain what credit reports contain, get free reports, and dispute errors
questions.intro: Credit reports show identifying information, credit accounts (cards, loans), balances, credit limits, payment history, inquiries, and certain collections. They do not include income, bank balances, race, religion, or medical details.
questions.question: Which item is generally on a credit report?

choices.text: Whether card payments were on time

questions.correct_answer: Whether card payments were on time
questions.feedback: Payment history on credit accounts is a core part of credit reports.

questions.section_skill: Explain what credit reports contain, get free reports, and dispute errors
questions.intro: If a report has an error, you can dispute it with the credit bureau (and the company that reported it). The bureau generally must investigate, usually within 30 days. An account you never opened can be a sign of identity theft.
questions.question: Jordan's report lists a credit card she never opened. What should she do?

choices.text: Ignore it, since reports are always correct
Pay off the card to make it go away
Dispute it and check for identity theft

questions.correct_answer: Dispute it and check for identity theft

misconceptions.B: Pays a debt that is not hers

questions.feedback: Disputing errors is free; an unknown account may mean identity theft.

questions.section_skill: Explain what credit reports contain, get free reports, and dispute errors
questions.intro: Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, only those with a "permissible purpose" can see your report: lenders, insurers, landlords, and employers (with your written permission), among others.
questions.question: Who may legally see Jordan's credit report?

choices.text: Any curious neighbor who wants to know

questions.correct_answer: A lender reviewing her application
questions.feedback: Lenders evaluating applications have a permissible purpose.

questions.intro: Your credit history shows how you have handled borrowing: which accounts you have, how much you owe, and whether you paid on time.
questions.question: What is a credit history?

choices.text: A list of every purchase a person has made with cash
A record of how a person has borrowed and repaid

questions.correct_answer: A record of how a person has borrowed and repaid
questions.feedback: Credit history tracks borrowing and repayment.

questions.intro: Credit accounts such as loans and credit cards are reported to credit bureaus. Cash and debit purchases usually are not.
questions.question: Which activity adds to a person's credit history?

choices.text: Repaying a car loan on time
Saving money in a piggy bank

questions.correct_answer: Repaying a car loan on time
questions.feedback: Loans and credit cards build credit history.

questions.intro: Past repayment behavior helps lenders estimate the risk that a borrower will not repay.
questions.question: Why do lenders look at credit history?

choices.text: To learn which stores a borrower likes best
To predict whether a borrower will repay

questions.correct_answer: To predict whether a borrower will repay
questions.feedback: Past repayment helps predict future repayment.

questions.intro: People with few or no credit accounts have "thin" files, which makes it harder for lenders to judge them.
questions.question: A student with no loans or cards applies for credit. What problem might she face?

choices.text: A "thin" credit file with little history to judge
Her report will show many late payments from the past
She will be approved for any amount
She has a perfect score by default

questions.correct_answer: A "thin" credit file with little history to judge
questions.feedback: No history makes approval harder, not easier.

questions.intro: Credit history can affect renting an apartment, insurance prices in many states, and some job applications (with written permission).
questions.question: Besides lenders, who else may check credit history (with permission when required)?
questions.correct_answer: Landlords and insurers
questions.feedback: Landlords and insurers may review credit information for permissible purposes.

questions.section_skill: Reading a credit report line by line
questions.intro: Credit report account lines show the creditor, limit or loan amount, balance, and payment status by month. Late payments are usually reported once they are 30 or more days past due.
questions.question: A report line shows: "Card A — limit $2,000 — balance $600 — status: 30 days late (March)". What does "30 days late" mean?

choices.text: The card was opened 30 days ago
The card has 30 days of interest-free time each month
A payment was at least 30 days past due in March

questions.correct_answer: A payment was at least 30 days past due in March
questions.feedback: A 30-day late payment was reported for March.

questions.section_skill: Reading a credit report line by line
questions.intro: A hard inquiry happens when a lender checks your credit because you applied for credit; it can lower scores slightly for a short time. Soft inquiries, such as checking your own report or prescreened offers, do not affect scores.
questions.question: A report shows two "hard inquiries" from lenders this month. What caused them?

choices.text: Receiving a preapproved offer in the mail

questions.correct_answer: Applications for new credit
questions.feedback: Hard inquiries come from credit applications.

questions.section_skill: Reading a credit report line by line
questions.intro: Soft inquiries, including checking your own credit, do not affect credit scores.
questions.question: Which inquiry does NOT affect a credit score?

choices.text: Applying for a private student loan

questions.correct_answer: Checking your own credit report
questions.feedback: Checking your own credit is a soft inquiry with no score impact.

questions.section_skill: Reading a credit report line by line
questions.intro: Paying a collection usually updates its status to "paid," but the record can remain for the reporting period allowed by law.
questions.question: A report shows a collection account that Ana paid in full 2 years ago. What should it show now?

choices.text: The collection, updated to show it was paid

questions.correct_answer: The collection, updated to show it was paid
questions.feedback: It should be updated as paid; it may remain on the report for the allowed time.

questions.section_skill: Reading a credit report line by line
questions.intro: Lenders choose which bureaus to report to, and reporting dates differ, so the three reports may not match exactly.
questions.question: Ana reviews her reports from all three bureaus. Why might they differ?

choices.text: One of them must be fake
Bureaus copy each other's reports exactly every day
Not every lender reports to every bureau

questions.correct_answer: Not every lender reports to every bureau
questions.feedback: Different reporting leads to differences; check all three.

questions.section_skill: Freezes, fraud alerts, and identity protection
questions.intro: A credit freeze (security freeze) restricts access to your credit report, so identity thieves cannot easily open new accounts in your name. Freezes are free at each bureau, and you can lift them temporarily when you apply for credit.
questions.question: What does a credit freeze do?

choices.text: It blocks most new lenders from seeing your report
It stops you from using your own debit card or checks

questions.correct_answer: It blocks most new lenders from seeing your report
questions.feedback: A freeze blocks most new-credit checks without affecting your score or existing accounts.

questions.section_skill: Freezes, fraud alerts, and identity protection
questions.intro: Since 2018, federal law has required the nationwide credit bureaus to place and lift credit freezes for free.
questions.question: How much does it cost to place a credit freeze at a nationwide bureau?

choices.text: Nothing; freezes are free by law
A fee of 1% of your total credit limit

questions.correct_answer: Nothing; freezes are free by law
questions.feedback: Freezes are free at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion.

questions.section_skill: Freezes, fraud alerts, and identity protection
questions.intro: You can lift a freeze temporarily for a specific time or lender, then it returns.
questions.question: Ana froze her credit and now wants to apply for a car loan. What should she do?

choices.text: Lift the freeze for a short time
Nothing; lenders can see frozen reports

questions.correct_answer: Lift the freeze for a short time
questions.feedback: A temporary lift lets the lender check her credit.

questions.section_skill: Freezes, fraud alerts, and identity protection
questions.intro: A fraud alert asks lenders to take extra steps to verify your identity before opening credit. A credit freeze blocks most access to your report.
questions.question: How is a fraud alert different from a credit freeze?

choices.text: A freeze costs money; an alert is free
They are identical; both close your current accounts
An alert asks for ID checks; a freeze blocks access

questions.correct_answer: An alert asks for ID checks; a freeze blocks access
questions.feedback: Alerts add verification; freezes restrict access.

questions.section_skill: Freezes, fraud alerts, and identity protection
questions.question: Which teen habit best protects future credit?

choices.text: Keeping a Social Security number private
Posting a full birth date and address online

questions.correct_answer: Keeping a Social Security number private
questions.feedback: Protecting your SSN and personal data prevents thieves from opening accounts in your name.

questions.section_skill: Explain the factors that affect credit scores and how scores affect borrowing costs
questions.intro: A credit score is a number (often 300–850) that summarizes credit risk based on a credit report. FICO's general weights: payment history about 35%, amounts owed about 30%, length of credit history about 15%, new credit about 10%, and credit mix about 10%. Other scoring models exist.
questions.question: In the widely used FICO model, which factor has the LARGEST weight?
questions.correct_answer: Payment history (about 35%)
questions.feedback: Paying on time matters most.

questions.section_skill: Explain the factors that affect credit scores and how scores affect borrowing costs
questions.intro: Credit scores affect the interest rates lenders offer. A higher score usually means a lower rate, which lowers monthly payments and total cost.
questions.question: Two applicants want a $20,000, 5-year car loan. Applicant A (strong credit) is offered 6% APR, with a $386.66 payment; Applicant B is offered 12% APR, with a $444.89 payment. How much more does B pay over 5 years?

questions.section_skill: Explain the factors that affect credit scores and how scores affect borrowing costs
questions.intro: Scores reward on-time payments and low balances compared with limits, and can drop with late payments, high balances, and many new applications.
questions.question: Which action is MOST likely to raise a credit score over time?

choices.text: Opening several new cards in one month

questions.correct_answer: Paying every bill on time
questions.feedback: Consistent on-time payments are the strongest positive factor.

questions.section_skill: Explain the factors that affect credit scores and how scores affect borrowing costs
questions.intro: Credit scores use only information in credit reports. Income, employment, savings, age, race, and where you live are not part of the score.
questions.question: Which is NOT used in calculating FICO credit scores?
questions.correct_answer: Income
questions.feedback: Income is not in credit reports, so it is not in the score (lenders may still ask about it).

questions.section_skill: Explain the factors that affect credit scores and how scores affect borrowing costs
questions.question: Ivy's FICO score is 780; Max's is 580. Which statement is MOST accurate?

choices.text: Max will pay lower rates, since lower is better
Max will likely face higher rates or denials

questions.correct_answer: Max will likely face higher rates or denials
questions.feedback: On the 300–850 scale, higher scores indicate lower risk and usually get better terms.

questions.section_skill: Percent weights and parts of a whole
questions.intro: Parts of a whole are added to find a combined share.
questions.question: If payment history is 35% of a score and amounts owed is 30%, together they make up what percent?

questions.section_skill: Percent weights and parts of a whole
questions.intro: Percents of the same whole can be compared directly.
questions.question: Which is larger: 15% or 10%?

questions.section_skill: Percent weights and parts of a whole
questions.question: Five factors weigh 35%, 30%, 15%, 10%, and 10%. What is their total?
questions.feedback: They add to 100%: the whole score model.

questions.section_skill: Percent weights and parts of a whole
questions.question: A score went from 650 to 700. By how many points did it rise?

questions.section_skill: Percent weights and parts of a whole
questions.intro: Length of credit history considers how long your accounts have been open, on average and for the oldest account.
questions.question: Which factor relates to how long accounts have been open?
questions.correct_answer: Length of credit history
questions.feedback: Length of credit history measures account age.

questions.intro: Landlords often review credit reports or scores because past bill-paying predicts rent payment.
questions.question: A landlord checks Tia's credit before approving an apartment. Why?

choices.text: To predict whether she will pay rent on time
To check her medical history and recent doctor visits

questions.correct_answer: To predict whether she will pay rent on time
questions.feedback: Credit history helps landlords predict on-time rent.

questions.intro: Many insurers use credit-based insurance scores to help set prices, where state law allows.
questions.question: In many states, auto insurers use credit-based insurance scores. What does this mean for drivers with weaker credit?
questions.correct_answer: They may pay higher premiums
questions.feedback: Weaker credit can raise premiums in states that allow this.

questions.intro: Employers may review credit reports (not scores) for some jobs, but federal law requires your written permission. Some states limit this further.
questions.question: An employer wants to check Tia's credit report for a job. What must happen first?

choices.text: The employer must lend Tia money

questions.correct_answer: Tia must give written permission
questions.feedback: Written permission is required for employment checks.

questions.intro: Over long loans, a small rate difference adds up: extra cost = monthly difference × number of payments.
questions.question: A 100-point lower score raises a $250,000 mortgage rate from 6.5% to 7.5%. Payments rise from $1,580 to $1,748 a month. How much more is paid over 30 years?

questions.intro: FICO and VantageScore both make several versions, and each bureau's data differs, so scores vary.
questions.question: Which statement about "credit scores" is MOST accurate?

choices.text: Different models give a person many scores
Everyone has one official score set by the government
Scores are the same at every bureau

questions.correct_answer: Different models give a person many scores
questions.feedback: Different models and bureaus produce different scores.

questions.intro: Checking your own report or score is a soft inquiry and never affects scores.
questions.question: Myth or fact: "Checking my own credit report lowers my score."

choices.text: Fact: every check lowers your score
Myth: your own check is a soft inquiry
Fact: each check lowers your score by about 50 points

questions.correct_answer: Myth: your own check is a soft inquiry
questions.feedback: Self-checks are soft inquiries; check as often as you like.

questions.intro: Card use is reported each month. Paying the full statement balance shows responsible use without paying interest.
questions.question: Myth or fact: "Carrying a small balance and paying interest helps your score."

choices.text: Myth: paying in full still shows on-time use
Fact: only balances over $1,000 count toward building credit
Fact: scores need debt to exist

questions.correct_answer: Myth: paying in full still shows on-time use
questions.feedback: You do not need to pay interest to build credit.

questions.intro: Credit scores use only information in credit reports.
questions.question: Myth or fact: "My income determines my credit score."

choices.text: Fact: higher income always means a higher score
Fact: scores are a percent of income
Myth: income is not in credit reports
Fact: only salaried workers have scores

questions.correct_answer: Myth: income is not in credit reports
questions.feedback: Income is not part of the score, though lenders consider it separately.

questions.intro: Closing a card removes its credit limit from your total available credit and may eventually shorten your credit history.
questions.question: Myth or fact: "Closing an old, unused card always raises my score."

choices.text: Fact: fewer cards always means higher scores
Fact: closed cards are deleted immediately
Fact: closing a card erases its late payments from your report
Myth: it can raise utilization and shorten history

questions.correct_answer: Myth: it can raise utilization and shorten history
questions.feedback: Closing a card can raise your utilization ratio and, over time, shorten your history.

questions.intro: Scoring models usually treat multiple inquiries for the same kind of loan (car, mortgage, student) within a short window as one, so you can shop for the best rate.
questions.question: Myth or fact: "Shopping for a car loan at several lenders within a short period ruins my score."

choices.text: Fact: each inquiry costs about 50 points every time
Myth: they usually count as one inquiry
Fact: you must never compare lenders
Fact: only the first lender counts

questions.correct_answer: Myth: they usually count as one inquiry
questions.feedback: Rate shopping within a short window is generally treated as a single inquiry.

questions.section_skill: Build a credit history with low utilization, on-time payments, and starter credit products
questions.intro: Credit utilization = card balances ÷ credit limits × 100. It is a major part of the "amounts owed" score factor. Lower utilization generally helps scores; a common guideline is to stay below about 30%, and lower is better.
questions.question: Tia's card has a $1,500 limit, and her statement balance is $450. What is her credit utilization?

questions.section_skill: Build a credit history with low utilization, on-time payments, and starter credit products
questions.intro: Overall utilization adds all balances and divides by all limits.
questions.question: Max has two cards: $300 balance on a $1,000 limit and $700 on a $2,500 limit. What is his overall utilization (nearest tenth)?

misconceptions.C: Divides by the larger limit only

questions.section_skill: Build a credit history with low utilization, on-time payments, and starter credit products
questions.intro: Starter options include a secured credit card (you put down a deposit that usually becomes your limit), a credit-builder loan (payments are saved for you and released at the end), and being added as an authorized user on a parent's card. Paying on time builds history.
questions.question: Leo has no credit history. Which product is designed to help someone start building credit?

choices.text: A secured credit card backed by a cash deposit
A savings account that comes with no card attached

questions.correct_answer: A secured credit card backed by a cash deposit

misconceptions.B: Usually not reported and very costly

questions.feedback: A secured card reports like a regular card but is backed by a deposit.

questions.section_skill: Build a credit history with low utilization, on-time payments, and starter credit products
questions.intro: An authorized user can use someone else's card. Many issuers report the account to the authorized user's credit file too, which can help, or hurt if the account is misused.
questions.question: Leo is added as an authorized user on his mother's card. Her account has a long on-time history and low utilization. What can this do?

choices.text: Make Leo responsible for her past debts
Give Leo his own separate credit limit and account
Help Leo's credit file show positive history

questions.correct_answer: Help Leo's credit file show positive history
questions.feedback: The account's positive history may appear on Leo's report.

questions.section_skill: Build a credit history with low utilization, on-time payments, and starter credit products
questions.question: Which plan builds credit with the LEAST cost?

choices.text: Carry a balance each month to show activity
Max out the card, then pay the minimum
Never use the card at all
Charge a small bill and pay it in full

questions.correct_answer: Charge a small bill and pay it in full
questions.feedback: Small, regular use paid in full builds history without interest.

questions.intro: Percent = part ÷ whole × 100.
questions.question: $200 is what percent of $1,000?

questions.intro: Part = percent × whole.
questions.question: A card has a $2,000 limit. What balance equals 10% utilization?
Which utilization is LOWEST?
questions.correct_answer: $100 of a $2,000 limit

questions.intro: Utilization is balance ÷ limit. A larger limit with the same balance makes the fraction smaller.
questions.question: If balances stay the same and a credit limit increases, what happens to utilization?
questions.correct_answer: It goes down
questions.feedback: A larger denominator lowers the percent.

questions.question: A card with a $500 limit has a $500 balance. What is utilization?

questions.section_skill: Credit-builder loans and secured cards in detail
questions.intro: With a credit-builder loan, the lender holds the loan amount in an account while you make payments. Payments are reported to bureaus, and you receive the money at the end. The cost is the interest and fees.
questions.question: A credit-builder loan of $600 is held in a savings account while Ana makes 12 payments of $52. What does she receive at the end, and what did it cost?
questions.feedback: 12 × $52 = $624 paid; she receives $600; cost $24.

questions.section_skill: Credit-builder loans and secured cards in detail
questions.intro: A secured card works like a regular credit card for utilization: balance ÷ limit.
questions.question: Leo opens a secured card with a $300 deposit and a $300 limit. He charges $30 a month and pays in full. What is his utilization each month?

misconceptions.C: Uses the deposit as a percent

questions.section_skill: Credit-builder loans and secured cards in detail
questions.intro: Many secured cards review accounts after a period of good use and may convert them to regular (unsecured) cards.
questions.question: After a year of on-time payments, some issuers "graduate" a secured card. What usually happens?

choices.text: The deposit is kept as a fee
It becomes a regular card; the deposit is returned
The card is closed and a penalty is charged to Leo
Leo must pay a new deposit

questions.correct_answer: It becomes a regular card; the deposit is returned
questions.feedback: Graduation returns the deposit and keeps the account history.

questions.section_skill: Credit-builder loans and secured cards in detail
questions.intro: A secured card helps build credit only if the issuer reports your payments to the credit bureaus.
questions.question: Which question should Leo ask before opening a secured card?

choices.text: Does the issuer report to all three credit bureaus?
Does the card have a cool design?
Can I use the card to get payday loans more easily?
Will it let me skip payments?

questions.correct_answer: Does the issuer report to all three credit bureaus?
questions.feedback: Reporting to the bureaus is what builds credit.

questions.section_skill: Credit-builder loans and secured cards in detail
questions.intro: When you pay the full balance every month, the APR does not affect your cost, but annual fees do.
questions.question: A secured card has a $49 annual fee and 25.99% APR; another has $0 fee and 28.99% APR. Leo will pay in full every month. Which is cheaper?

choices.text: The $49-fee card, because its APR is lower

questions.correct_answer: The $0-fee card

misconceptions.A: APR does not matter if paid in full

questions.feedback: Paying in full means no interest, so the annual fee is the only cost.

questions.intro: The key habits for building credit are on-time payment, low balances, and few new applications.
questions.question: Which step comes FIRST in a safe credit-building plan for a student?

choices.text: Apply for five cards at once
Spend up to the limit each month to show activity
Set up autopay for the full statement balance

questions.correct_answer: Set up autopay for the full statement balance
questions.feedback: Autopay in full prevents late payments and interest from day one.

questions.intro: Card issuers usually report the balance shown on your statement. Paying before the statement closes lowers the reported balance and utilization.
questions.question: Tia's statement balance would be $480 on a $600 limit (80%). She pays $400 BEFORE the statement closes. What utilization is reported?
questions.correct_answer: About 13%

questions.intro: Late payments of 30 days or more are usually reported to the bureaus and can stay on a credit report for years.
questions.question: Which habit could LOWER Tia's score during her first year?
questions.correct_answer: Missing a payment by 30+ days
questions.feedback: A 30-day late payment is reported and can hurt a score for years.

questions.intro: Utilization = balance ÷ limit.
questions.question: After a year, Tia's issuer offers a higher limit with no fee. If her spending stays the same, what effect does accepting it usually have?
questions.correct_answer: Lower utilization
questions.feedback: The same balance on a larger limit is a smaller percent, as long as spending does not rise.

questions.intro: You can get free credit reports at AnnualCreditReport.com, and many banks and card issuers show a free score.
questions.question: Which is the BEST way to check progress on building credit?

choices.text: Check free reports and scores regularly
Ask friends what their scores are
Apply for loans now and then to see if approved

questions.correct_answer: Check free reports and scores regularly
questions.feedback: Free reports and scores show progress without cost or inquiries.

questions.set_title: Saving versus investing: risk and return
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Distinguish saving from investing and explain the relationship between risk and return
questions.intro: Saving means setting money aside in safe, easy-to-reach places, such as insured bank accounts, for short-term goals and emergencies. Investing means buying assets, such as stocks, bonds, or funds, that may grow over time but can also lose value. Investments are not FDIC insured.
questions.question: Which statement best describes the difference between saving and investing?

choices.text: Saving and investing are two words for the same thing
Investing is guaranteed to earn more than saving every year
Saving always loses money, while investing never does
Saving keeps money safe and available; investing seeks growth but can lose value

questions.correct_answer: Saving keeps money safe and available; investing seeks growth but can lose value
questions.feedback: Savings protect value and access; investments aim for growth with the risk of loss.

questions.set_title: Saving versus investing: risk and return
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Distinguish saving from investing and explain the relationship between risk and return
questions.intro: Time horizon is how long until you need the money. Money needed soon should not be exposed to market drops. Long horizons give investments time to recover from downturns.
questions.question: Which goal is generally BETTER suited to investing than to a savings account?

choices.text: An emergency fund that must be available next week
Rent due at the start of next month
A car repair expected in two months

questions.correct_answer: Retirement in 40 years
questions.feedback: Long time horizons suit investing; short-term needs suit savings.

questions.set_title: Saving versus investing: risk and return
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Distinguish saving from investing and explain the relationship between risk and return
questions.intro: Risk is the chance that an investment's results will differ from what you expect, including losing money. In general, investments with higher expected returns have bigger ups and downs. Past averages do not guarantee future results.
questions.question: Investment A has averaged 3% a year with small ups and downs. Investment B has averaged 9% a year but sometimes lost 30% in a year. What does this illustrate?

choices.text: Investment B is guaranteed to earn 9% every year
Investment A can never lose any money at all
Higher potential return usually comes with higher risk
Risk and return are unrelated to each other

questions.correct_answer: Higher potential return usually comes with higher risk

misconceptions.A: Treats an average as a guarantee

questions.feedback: The higher-return investment comes with larger swings, including big losses.

questions.set_title: Saving versus investing: risk and return
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Distinguish saving from investing and explain the relationship between risk and return
questions.intro: Percent return = (ending value − starting value) ÷ starting value × 100.
questions.question: A stock fund rose from $50 to $58 a share in a year. What was the percent return (no dividends)?

misconceptions.A: Uses the dollar gain as a percent
misconceptions.D: Gives the ending value as a percent

questions.set_title: Saving versus investing: risk and return
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Distinguish saving from investing and explain the relationship between risk and return
questions.question: Which is TRUE about money invested in a stock fund through a brokerage account?

choices.text: It is FDIC insured up to $250,000, like a bank savings account
It can lose value and is not FDIC insured
It always keeps at least its starting value

questions.section_skill: Explain how bonds work and calculate bond interest
questions.intro: A bond is a loan from the investor to an issuer, such as a company, a city, or the U.S. government. The issuer promises to pay interest (the coupon) on a schedule and repay the face value at maturity. Bonds are investments, not deposits, and can lose value.

choices.text: Lends money to the issuer in return for interest and repayment
Buys ownership in the issuer and a vote at meetings
Opens an insured deposit at a bank branch
Pays a fee for the right to buy stock later

questions.set_title: Bonds: lending to governments and companies
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Explain how bonds work and calculate bond interest

choices.text: It stays exactly at face value no matter what
It turns into a 5% bond automatically

questions.question: Which bond generally has the LOWEST risk of default?

choices.text: A bond from a new company with heavy debt
A "junk" bond with a low credit rating
A bond from a company that recently missed payments

choices.text: What does it hold, and what does it cost each year?
Did it have the best return last month?

questions.correct_answer: What does it hold, and what does it cost each year?
questions.feedback: Holdings and costs matter most for long-term results.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Explain diversification and asset allocation and compute a portfolio's weighted return
questions.intro: Diversification means spreading money across many investments so that a problem with one has a smaller effect on the whole. It can be across companies, industries, countries, and types of assets (stocks, bonds, cash). Diversification lowers risk but cannot eliminate it or guarantee against loss.
questions.question: Which portfolio is MOST diversified?

choices.text: A total market index fund plus a bond index fund
Shares of a single restaurant chain and its supplier

questions.correct_answer: A total market index fund plus a bond index fund
questions.feedback: Thousands of stocks plus bonds spread risk widely.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Explain diversification and asset allocation and compute a portfolio's weighted return
questions.intro: Asset allocation is how a portfolio is divided among asset classes such as stocks, bonds, and cash. A portfolio's return is the weighted average: (weight × return) for each part, added together.
questions.question: Jen's portfolio is 60% stocks and 40% bonds. Stocks return 8% and bonds 3% this year. What is the portfolio's return?

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Explain diversification and asset allocation and compute a portfolio's weighted return
questions.question: Which statement about diversification is TRUE?

choices.text: A diversified portfolio cannot lose value
It reduces the impact of any single investment but cannot prevent all losses
Diversification guarantees a profit every year
Owning more shares of one stock is diversification

questions.correct_answer: It reduces the impact of any single investment but cannot prevent all losses

misconceptions.A: Assumes a diversified investment cannot lose value

questions.feedback: Broad market declines can still lower a diversified portfolio.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Explain diversification and asset allocation and compute a portfolio's weighted return
questions.question: Jen has $10,000 invested: 60% stocks, 40% bonds. How much is in stocks?

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Explain diversification and asset allocation and compute a portfolio's weighted return
questions.intro: A longer time horizon allows more time to recover from stock market declines, so younger investors often hold more stocks. People nearing their goal often shift toward bonds and cash.
questions.question: Generally, which allocation fits a 20-year-old saving for retirement better than a 70-year-old retiree?

choices.text: More stocks, because the time horizon is longer
All cash, because young people cannot handle risk
All bonds, because stocks are illegal for young investors
Exactly the same allocation for everyone

questions.correct_answer: More stocks, because the time horizon is longer
questions.feedback: Longer horizons can usually tolerate more stock market risk.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: When all your money depends on one thing, a problem with that thing affects everything. Spreading out reduces the damage.
questions.question: A fruit stand sells only bananas. A banana shortage hits. What happens?
questions.correct_answer: Its whole business suffers
questions.feedback: Depending on one product concentrates risk.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.question: A second stand sells bananas, apples, and oranges. The banana shortage hits. What happens?

choices.text: Only part of its business suffers

questions.correct_answer: Only part of its business suffers
questions.feedback: Selling several fruits spreads the risk.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.question: Which saying describes diversification?

choices.text: "A penny saved is a penny earned."
"Don't put all your eggs in one basket."

questions.correct_answer: "Don't put all your eggs in one basket."
questions.feedback: Spreading eggs across baskets limits the damage if one falls.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Asset classes are broad types of investments, such as stocks, bonds, and cash.
questions.question: Owning stocks AND bonds is diversification across what?
questions.correct_answer: Asset classes
questions.feedback: Stocks and bonds are different asset classes.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Percent of an amount = amount × rate as a decimal.
questions.question: What is 40% of $5,000?

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Over time, investments grow at different rates, so a portfolio drifts away from its target allocation. Rebalancing means buying or selling to return to the target.
questions.question: Jen's target is 60% stocks, 40% bonds on $10,000. After a strong year, she has $7,200 in stocks and $3,800 in bonds. What percent is in stocks now (nearest whole)?
questions.feedback: Total $11,000; $7,200 ÷ $11,000 ≈ 65.5%, about 65% (rounding down to whole).

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Target amount = total value × target percent.
questions.question: To rebalance $11,000 to 60% stocks, what should the stock amount be?

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Amount to move = current amount − target amount.
questions.question: Using a $6,600 stock target, how much stock should Jen sell (moving it to bonds)?

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Without rebalancing, a portfolio can become riskier than intended as stocks grow.
questions.question: Why rebalance?

choices.text: Because the law requires it each month
To keep risk at the level the investor chose

questions.correct_answer: To keep risk at the level the investor chose
questions.feedback: Rebalancing restores the chosen risk level.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Selling investments at a gain in a taxable account can create capital gains taxes.
questions.question: Instead of selling, Jen could rebalance by directing new contributions to bonds. Why might that be helpful in a taxable account?

choices.text: It can avoid selling and creating taxable gains
It is required by the IRS

questions.correct_answer: It can avoid selling and creating taxable gains
questions.feedback: Using new money to rebalance can avoid realizing gains.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Diversification works best when investments do not all move together. Assets that move the same way give little protection; assets that move differently reduce overall swings.
questions.question: Two stocks always rise and fall together. Does owning both diversify much?

choices.text: Yes, because there are two of them
Not much, because they move the same way

questions.correct_answer: Not much, because they move the same way
questions.feedback: Investments that move together provide little diversification.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: High-quality bonds often behave differently from stocks, especially in downturns, though not always.
questions.question: Which pair is more likely to diversify a stock-heavy portfolio?

choices.text: Two stock funds holding the same companies

questions.correct_answer: Stocks and high-quality bonds
questions.feedback: High-quality bonds often move differently from stocks.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Funds that track the same index hold the same companies, so owning several adds little diversification.
questions.question: Sam owns three different S&P 500 index funds. Is he well diversified across funds?

choices.text: Not really; the three funds hold almost the same stocks
Yes, because each has a different name
No, because index funds hold one stock

questions.correct_answer: Not really; the three funds hold almost the same stocks
questions.feedback: Overlapping funds add little real diversification.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Market risk affects nearly all stocks at once; diversification mainly reduces the risk of individual companies or industries.
questions.question: In a severe market crash, many stocks fall together. What does this show about diversification across stocks?

choices.text: Bonds always fall more than stocks

questions.correct_answer: It cannot remove market-wide risk
questions.feedback: Market-wide declines affect even diversified stock portfolios.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Target-date funds hold a mix of stock and bond funds and become more conservative over time.
questions.question: A target-date fund automatically shifts from stocks toward bonds as the target year approaches. What problem does it solve?

choices.text: It guarantees no losses before the target year
It manages allocation and rebalancing for you

questions.correct_answer: It manages allocation and rebalancing for you
questions.feedback: Target-date funds automate allocation changes over time.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Place basic investment orders and explain market orders, limit orders, and the bid-ask spread
questions.intro: To buy an investment, you place an order with your broker. A market order asks to buy or sell right away at the best available price. It usually executes quickly, but the exact price is not guaranteed and can differ from the last price you saw, especially in fast markets.
questions.question: Kai places a MARKET order to buy 10 shares. What does this mean?

choices.text: Buy only if the price falls to a set amount
Buy promptly at the best price available, which is not guaranteed
Buy at yesterday's closing price, guaranteed
Buy only after the market closes for the day

questions.correct_answer: Buy promptly at the best price available, which is not guaranteed
questions.feedback: Market orders prioritize speed, not a guaranteed price.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Place basic investment orders and explain market orders, limit orders, and the bid-ask spread
questions.intro: A limit order sets the most you will pay (to buy) or the least you will accept (to sell). It executes only at the limit price or better, so it may not execute at all.
questions.question: Lia places a LIMIT order to buy at $50. The stock is trading at $52. What happens?

choices.text: The order fills only if the price falls to $50 or lower
It buys at $50 no matter what the market price is

questions.correct_answer: The order fills only if the price falls to $50 or lower

misconceptions.D: Thinks the limit forces a price

questions.feedback: A buy limit at $50 fills only at $50 or less.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Place basic investment orders and explain market orders, limit orders, and the bid-ask spread
questions.intro: The bid is the highest price buyers are offering; the ask is the lowest price sellers will accept. Buyers usually pay the ask, and sellers receive the bid. The difference is the bid-ask spread.
questions.question: A stock shows: bid $49.95, ask $50.05. If Omar places a market order to BUY, about what price will he pay?
questions.feedback: A market buy order typically fills near the ask, $50.05.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Place basic investment orders and explain market orders, limit orders, and the bid-ask spread
questions.intro: The bid-ask spread = ask − bid. Narrow spreads mean lower trading costs.
questions.question: Using the bid of $49.95 and ask of $50.05, what is the bid-ask spread?

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: A trade happens when a buyer and a seller agree on a price. Exchanges match buyers and sellers.
questions.question: In any market, who decides the price of a trade?

choices.text: A buyer and a seller who agree

questions.correct_answer: A buyer and a seller who agree
questions.feedback: Trades happen at prices both sides accept.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: The asking price is what a seller wants; the offer (bid) is what a buyer will pay.
questions.question: A seller asks $20 for a used game. A buyer offers $18. What must happen for a sale?

choices.text: One of them changes their price until they agree

questions.correct_answer: One of them changes their price until they agree
questions.feedback: No trade occurs until the bid and ask meet.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: An order tells your broker what to buy or sell, how many shares (or dollars), and at what kind of price.
questions.question: What is an "order" when investing?

choices.text: An instruction to a broker to buy or sell

questions.correct_answer: An instruction to a broker to buy or sell
questions.feedback: Orders are trading instructions.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: The bid is what buyers offer; the ask is what sellers accept.
questions.question: Which tells you the LOWEST price a seller will accept right now?
questions.correct_answer: The ask
questions.feedback: The ask is the lowest current selling price.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Limit orders for selling and stop orders
questions.intro: A sell limit order sets the minimum price you will accept. It executes only at that price or higher.
questions.question: Ana owns a stock trading at $40. She places a SELL limit order at $45. When can it execute?

choices.text: Only if the price rises to $45 or higher
Only if the price falls to $45 or lower

questions.correct_answer: Only if the price rises to $45 or higher
questions.feedback: A sell limit at $45 fills at $45 or more.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Limit orders for selling and stop orders
questions.intro: A stop order becomes a market order once the stop price is reached, so the sale price can be worse than the stop price in a fast-moving market.
questions.question: A stop-loss (stop) order to sell at $35 becomes a market order when the price falls to $35. The price gaps down overnight to $30. What might happen?

choices.text: It may sell near $30, below the $35 stop price

questions.correct_answer: It may sell near $30, below the $35 stop price
questions.feedback: Once triggered, it is a market order and fills at the next available price.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Limit orders for selling and stop orders
questions.question: Which order type risks NOT executing at all?

choices.text: A market order in a heavily traded stock
A buy of a widely traded index ETF at market
A market sell during trading hours

questions.correct_answer: A limit order
questions.feedback: Limit orders execute only at the limit or better, so they may never fill.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Limit orders for selling and stop orders
questions.intro: Orders can be day orders (expire at the end of the trading day) or good-'til-canceled (stay open longer, often up to a time limit set by the broker).
questions.question: An order marked "good 'til canceled" (GTC) means…

choices.text: it is canceled at market open
it stays open until filled or canceled, up to the broker's time limit

questions.correct_answer: it stays open until filled or canceled, up to the broker's time limit
questions.feedback: GTC orders remain open until filled, canceled, or they expire under the broker's rules.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Limit orders for selling and stop orders
questions.intro: For heavily traded funds with narrow spreads, market orders usually fill close to the quoted price, and a limit order at the ask adds price protection.
questions.question: A long-term investor buys a widely traded index ETF with a narrow spread. Which order type is often reasonable?

choices.text: A limit order near the current ask, or a market order
A stop-loss order far below the price
No order; ETFs cannot be bought

questions.correct_answer: A limit order near the current ask, or a market order
questions.feedback: Either works for liquid ETFs; a limit at the ask adds price protection.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: A wide spread is a hidden trading cost: buying at the ask and selling at the bid loses the spread on each share.
questions.question: A thinly traded stock has a bid of $9.50 and an ask of $10.50. Kai buys 100 shares at the ask and immediately sells at the bid. How much does he lose?
questions.feedback: Spread $1.00 × 100 shares = $100.

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders
questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.intro: Prices can move quickly at the opening because of overnight news.
questions.question: Why might placing a market order right when the market opens be risky?

choices.text: The price is fixed at the open
Prices can swing sharply at the open
Market orders do not work in the morning

questions.set_title: Placing an order: market and limit orders

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Calculate investment fees and explain how they reduce long-term returns
questions.intro: An expense ratio is the yearly cost of owning a fund, expressed as a percent of the money invested. It is taken out of the fund's assets automatically, so you never see a bill, but it lowers your return. Annual cost = amount invested × expense ratio.
questions.question: A fund has an expense ratio of 0.50%. How much does it cost per year on a $8,000 investment?

misconceptions.C: Uses the percent as dollars per hundred

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Calculate investment fees and explain how they reduce long-term returns
questions.intro: Comparing expense ratios in dollars shows how much a fee difference costs you each year.
questions.question: Two funds hold similar investments. Fund A charges 0.04%; Fund B charges 1.04%. On $20,000, how much more does Fund B cost per year?
questions.feedback: Difference 1.00% × $20,000 = $200 per year.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Calculate investment fees and explain how they reduce long-term returns
questions.intro: Fees reduce returns every year, and the lost growth compounds. A difference that looks small each year can become large over decades.
questions.question: $10,000 grows for 30 years at 7% a year before fees. With a 0.05% fee, it grows to about $75,063; with a 0.75% fee, about $61,641. How much does the higher fee cost over 30 years?
questions.correct_answer: About $13,422

misconceptions.A: Uses one year of the fee difference
misconceptions.B: Uses 30 years of simple fees on $10,000

questions.feedback: $75,063 − $61,641 ≈ $13,422 lost to the higher fee.

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Calculate total and annualized returns, compare nominal and real returns, and describe volatility
questions.intro: Total return is the percent change over the whole period. The annualized (compound) return is the steady yearly rate that would produce the same result: (ending ÷ starting)^(1 ÷ years) − 1.
questions.question: Mia invested $1,000, and five years later it is worth $1,610.51 with no additions. Which annual growth rate, compounded, produces this?

misconceptions.C: Divides total growth by 5 years (simple average)

questions.feedback: 1,000 × 1.10^5 = 1,610.51, so the annualized return is 10% (total return 61.05%).

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Calculate total and annualized returns, compare nominal and real returns, and describe volatility
questions.intro: Total return = (ending − starting) ÷ starting × 100.
questions.question: Mia's investment rose from $1,000 to $1,610.51. What is the TOTAL return?

misconceptions.D: Gives the ending value as a percent

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Calculate total and annualized returns, compare nominal and real returns, and describe volatility
questions.intro: The nominal return is the stated return. The real return adjusts for inflation and shows the change in purchasing power: real return ≈ nominal return − inflation (more precisely, (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1).
questions.question: An investment returned 8% last year while inflation was 3%. What was the approximate REAL return?
questions.correct_answer: About 5%

questions.unit_title: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.section_skill: Calculate total and annualized returns, compare nominal and real returns, and describe volatility
questions.intro: Volatility describes how much returns vary from year to year. Investments with the same average return can have very different volatility; more volatility usually means more risk.
questions.question: Fund X's yearly returns: 6%, 7%, 5%, 6%. Fund Y's: 20%, −10%, 25%, −11%. Both averaged 6%. Which is more volatile?

choices.text: Neither; volatility is the same as average return

questions.correct_answer: Fund Y

questions.set_title: Renting versus owning, and what a mortgage is
questions.section_skill: Compare renting and owning and explain the parts of a mortgage
questions.intro: A mortgage is a loan used to buy a home. The home is collateral: if the borrower does not repay, the lender can foreclose (take and sell the home). Mortgages usually last 15 or 30 years and are repaid with monthly payments of principal and interest.

choices.text: A monthly rent payment to a landlord
Insurance that protects a home from fire
A loan to buy a home, with the home as collateral
A savings account for a down payment

questions.correct_answer: A loan to buy a home, with the home as collateral
questions.feedback: A mortgage is a home loan secured by the home.
